**UnitedHealth Group Incorporated** is an American [multinational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation") [for-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/For-profit "For-profit") company based in [Eden Prairie, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eden_Prairie,_Minnesota "Eden Prairie, Minnesota"), specializing in [health insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_insurance "Health insurance") and health care services. Selling insurance products under [UnitedHealthcare](#UnitedHealthcare), and health care services under the [Optum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optum "Optum") brand, it is the [world's fourth-largest company by revenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_companies_by_revenue "List of largest companies by revenue") and the largest health care company by revenue. The company is ranked fourth on the 2026 [*Fortune* Global 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_Global_500 "Fortune Global 500").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

UnitedHealth Group had a [market capitalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") of more than $400 billion as of year-end 2025.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The company is the largest health insurer in the United States, insuring over 50 million people,[[8]](#cite_note-8)[[9]](#cite_note-9) and operates globally.[[10]](#cite_note-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11)

UnitedHealth Group has faced numerous[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14) investigations, lawsuits, and fines, including [SEC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission") enforcement for stock option backdating, [Medicare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States) "Medicare (United States)") over-billing, unfair claims practices, mental health treatment denials, and [anticompetitive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anti-competitive_practices "Anti-competitive practices") behavior.

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

### 1970s–1990s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1970s–1990s")]

UnitedHealth Group originated in late 1974, when Minnesota-based Charter Med Incorporated was founded by [Richard Taylor Burke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_T._Burke "Richard T. Burke"). It originally processed claims for doctors at the Hennepin County Medical Society.[[15]](#cite_note-15) UnitedHealthcare Corporation was founded in 1977 to purchase Charter Med and create a network-based health plan for seniors.[[16]](#cite_note-16) It became a publicly traded company in 1984 and changed its name to UnitedHealth Group in 1998.[[17]](#cite_note-17)

In 1988, UnitedHealthcare started its first [pharmacy benefit management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmacy_benefit_manager "Pharmacy benefit manager"), through its [Diversified Pharmaceutical Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diversified_Pharmaceutical_Services "Diversified Pharmaceutical Services") subsidiary. It managed pharmacy benefits delivered both through retail pharmacies and mail. The subsidiary was sold to [SmithKline Beecham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SmithKline_Beecham "SmithKline Beecham") in 1994 for $2.3 billion.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

In 1994, UnitedHealthcare acquired Ramsey-HMO, a Florida insurer.[[19]](#cite_note-19) In 1995, the company acquired The MetraHealth Companies Inc. for $1.65 billion. MetraHealth was a privately held company formed by combining the group healthcare operations of [The Travelers Companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Travelers_Companies "The Travelers Companies") and [MetLife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MetLife "MetLife"). In 1996, UnitedHealthcare acquired HealthWise of America, which operated HMOs in Arkansas, Maryland, Kentucky and Tennessee.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In 1998, the company was reorganized as the [holding company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_company "Holding company") for hitherto independent companies UnitedHealthcare, Ovations, Uniprise, Specialized Care Services, and Ingenix and rebranded as "UnitedHealth Group". Also in 1998, UnitedHealth Group acquired HealthPartners of Arizona, operator of Arizona's largest [AHCCCS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_Health_Care_Cost_Containment_System "Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System") provider.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

### 2000s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2000s")]

In 2001, EverCare, a UnitedHealth Group subsidiary, merged with LifeMark Health Plans[[22]](#cite_note-22) In 2002, UnitedHealth Group acquired GeoAccess and Medicaid insurance company AmeriChoice.[[23]](#cite_note-23) In 2003, UnitedHealth Group acquired Mid Atlantic Medical Services, an insurer serving Maryland, Washington D.C., Virginia, Delaware and West Virginia.[[24]](#cite_note-24) Also in 2003, UnitedHealth Group acquired Golden Rule Financial, a provider of health savings accounts.[[25]](#cite_note-25) On July 21, 2003, Exante Bank started operating in Salt Lake City, Utah, as a Utah state-chartered industrial loan corporation. It changed its name to OptumHealth Bank in 2008[[26]](#cite_note-26) and to [Optum Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optum_Bank "Optum Bank") in 2012.

In April 2004, UnitedHealth Group acquired Touchpoint Health Plan, a Wisconsin health plan.[[27]](#cite_note-27) In July 2004, the company acquired [Oxford Health Plans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford_Health_Plans "Oxford Health Plans").[[28]](#cite_note-28)

In December 2005, the company acquired [PacifiCare Health Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PacifiCare_Health_Systems "PacifiCare Health Systems").[[29]](#cite_note-29) It agreed to divest parts of PacifiCare's commercial health insurance business in [Tucson, Arizona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tucson,_Arizona "Tucson, Arizona") and [Boulder, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boulder,_Colorado "Boulder, Colorado") to satisfy [antitrust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antitrust "Antitrust") regulator concerns, and also agreed to end its network access agreement with [Blue Shield of California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Shield_of_California "Blue Shield of California"). The Tucson business was sold to Cigna.[[30]](#cite_note-30) The company acquired Prescription Solutions, another pharmacy benefits manager, as part of its acquisition of PacifiCare Health Systems.[[31]](#cite_note-2005_Annual_Report-31) This business was later rebranded OptumRx.

In February 2006, the company acquired [John Deere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Deere "John Deere") Health Care.[[32]](#cite_note-32)[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34) The same year, [William W. McGuire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_W._McGuire "William W. McGuire") stepped down as chairman and director due to his involvement in the employee stock options scandal.[[35]](#cite_note-35) He was replaced by CEO [Stephen Hemsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_J._Hemsley "Stephen J. Hemsley") who had served as president and COO and a member of the board of directors. McGuire's exit compensation from UnitedHealth was anticipated to be $1.1 billion,[[36]](#cite_note-36) but he only received $618 million after returning $420 million in stock options.[[37]](#cite_note-37)

In February 2008, the company acquired Sierra Health Services for $2.6 billion.[[38]](#cite_note-38) As part of the transaction, to obtain regulatory approval, 25,000 customers were sold to [Humana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humana "Humana").[[39]](#cite_note-39) In July 2009, UnitedHealth Group agreed to acquire [Health Net](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Net "Health Net")'s Northeast licensed subsidiaries for up to $570 million in payments spread out over two years.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

### 2010s

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2010s")]

Through 2010 and into 2011, senior executives of the company met monthly with executives of other health insurers to limit the effect of the health care reform law.[[41]](#cite_note-41) In July 2010, Ingenix acquired Picis Clinical Solutions, Inc., a health information provider for the high-acuity areas of hospitals.[[42]](#cite_note-42)[[43]](#cite_note-43) In 2011, Logistics Health, Inc. of [La Crosse, Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Crosse,_Wisconsin "La Crosse, Wisconsin"), was acquired by OptumHealth.[[44]](#cite_note-44) In September 2014, the office buildings where LHI is based were sold to UnitedHealth Group for $45 million.[[45]](#cite_note-45)[[46]](#cite_note-46) In February 2012, the company acquired XLHealth, a sponsor of [Medicare Advantage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_Advantage "Medicare Advantage") health plans with a primary focus on medicare recipients with special needs such as those with chronic illness and those eligible for Medicaid ("dual eligibles").[[47]](#cite_note-47)[[48]](#cite_note-48) In October 2012, UnitedHealth Group and Amil Participações, one of the biggest Brazilian health insurance companies, completed the first phase of their merger.[[49]](#cite_note-49)[[50]](#cite_note-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/eb/LHI_buildings.jpg/250px-LHI_buildings.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LHI_buildings.jpg)

Former LHI (now Optum Serve) buildings in [La Crosse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Crosse,_Wisconsin "La Crosse, Wisconsin")

In February 2014, [Optum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optum "Optum") secured a [majority stake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_stake "Majority stake") in the Washington, D.C.–based startup Audax Health.[[52]](#cite_note-Farr-52) Audax's CEO, [Grant Verstandig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grant_Verstandig?action=edit&redlink=1 "Grant Verstandig (page does not exist)"), continued running the firm alongside [COO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_operating_officer "Chief operating officer") David Ko.[[52]](#cite_note-Farr-52) In October 2014, Optum Health acquired the health services unit of [Alere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alere "Alere") for $600 million cash.[[53]](#cite_note-53)

In March 2015, it was announced that [CatamaranRx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catamaran_Corporation "Catamaran Corporation") would be acquired by OptumRx.[[54]](#cite_note-54) In April 2016, the company announced it was pulling out of all but a "handful" of state healthcare exchanges provided under [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") and will continue to sell only in three states in 2017.[[55]](#cite_note-55)[[56]](#cite_note-56)

In 2017, UnitedHealth's Optum unit acquired Rally Health,[[57]](#cite_note-57) a company started by Audax Health's executives.[[58]](#cite_note-Rauber-58) Prior to acquisition, in 2015, UnitedHealth supported Rally Health as a majority investor,[[59]](#cite_note-59) and through enrolling more than 5 million UnitedHealth policy holders in Rally Health's flagship product, Rally.[[58]](#cite_note-Rauber-58)[[60]](#cite_note-60)[[nt 1]](#cite_note-61) The close relations between UnitedHealth, Audax Health and Rally Health follows a close personal relationship between Grant Verstandig (Audax and Rally) and UnitedHealth's [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_(corporate_title) "President (corporate title)") and [CFO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CFO "CFO") at the time, David Wichmann.[[61]](#cite_note-62)

In June 2019, UnitedHealth's [Optum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optum "Optum") division acquired DaVita Medical Group from [DaVita, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DaVita "DaVita") for $4.3 billion.[[62]](#cite_note-63)[[63]](#cite_note-64)[[64]](#cite_note-65) That year, the company also agreed to acquire Equian for $3.2 billion.[[65]](#cite_note-66)[[66]](#cite_note-67)[[67]](#cite_note-68) On June 19, 2019, UnitedHealth acquired the online [patient community platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Platform_as_a_service "Platform as a service") [PatientsLikeMe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PatientsLikeMe "PatientsLikeMe") for an undisclosed amount and it will be incorporated into UnitedHealth Group's research division.[[68]](#cite_note-69)

In November 2019, [Andrew Witty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Witty "Andrew Witty") was named president of UnitedHealth Group, in addition to his role as chief executive of the company's Optum division.[[69]](#cite_note-70)

### 2020s–present

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2020s–present")]

UnitedHealth announced in March 2022 that it would acquire LHC Group for $5.4 billion. The deal will expand its home health capabilities by combining LHC's services with UnitedHealth's Optum unit.[[70]](#cite_note-71)

In 2022, UnitedHealth Group said there would be no out-of-pocket costs for [albuterol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albuterol "Albuterol"), [epinephrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epinephrine "Epinephrine"), [glucagon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glucagon "Glucagon"), [insulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insulin "Insulin"), and [naloxone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naloxone "Naloxone") for fully insured members starting in 2023. The discounts were guaranteed for less than a quarter of UnitedHealthcare's membership and did not extend to those enrolled in UHC's [Medicare Advantage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_Advantage "Medicare Advantage") and [Medicaid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicaid "Medicaid") plans.[[71]](#cite_note-72)

In 2023, UnitedHealthGroup announced it would move its headquarters from Minnetonka to [Eden Prairie, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eden_Prairie,_Minnesota "Eden Prairie, Minnesota").[[72]](#cite_note-73)

In February 2024, UnitedHealth Group completed the sale of its operations in Brazil.[[73]](#cite_note-74)

In January 2021, UnitedHealth announced the acquisition of [Change Healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Change_Healthcare "Change Healthcare"), the largest health payments platform in the US, which the [US Justice Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Justice_Department "US Justice Department") tried to block on antitrust grounds in February 2022; the sale went through by September.[[74]](#cite_note-75)[[75]](#cite_note-ReutersAntitrust-76) 18 months later, in February 2024, the subsidiary was brought completely down by the [2024 Change Healthcare ransomware attack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Change_Healthcare_ransomware_attack "2024 Change Healthcare ransomware attack"), and the Justice Department announced that it was opening a new antitrust and [Medicare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States) "Medicare (United States)") overcharging probe.[[75]](#cite_note-ReutersAntitrust-76) Despite making a ransomware payment, services remained down or incomplete for months. The CEO, Andrew Witty, was called before the [US House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_House "US House") and [US Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Senate "US Senate") to testify about the cyberattack and DoJ concerns.[[76]](#cite_note-77) In late April 2024, the Senate held a hearing concerning the cyberattack and UnitedHealth's response. Andrew Witty went before the Senate stating that there needed to be a strong digital security system in place along with an adequate backup plan. UnitedHealth revealed the hackers did gain access to patient information, but the Senate was informed the company is not yet aware of the extent of the data breach.[[77]](#cite_note-78)

#### Killing of Brian Thompson

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Killing of Brian Thompson")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/UnitedHealthcare_Corporate_Headquarters%2C_December_8_2024_%2854191437643%29.jpg/250px-UnitedHealthcare_Corporate_Headquarters%2C_December_8_2024_%2854191437643%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:UnitedHealthcare_Corporate_Headquarters,_December_8_2024_(54191437643).jpg)

Police outside the corporate headquarters in [Minnetonka, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnetonka,_Minnesota "Minnetonka, Minnesota"), on December 8, 2024

On December 4, 2024, Brian Thompson, the CEO of UnitedHealth Group's insurance [subsidiary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsidiary "Subsidiary") UnitedHealthcare, was [killed in a shooting in New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Killing_of_Brian_Thompson "Killing of Brian Thompson").[[78]](#cite_note-Lukpat-79)[[79]](#cite_note-80) The shooting occurred outside the [New York Hilton Midtown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Hilton_Midtown "New York Hilton Midtown"), where UnitedHealth Group was hosting an investor event.[[78]](#cite_note-Lukpat-79) Reactions to the shooting on social media were defined by resentment and criticism of UnitedHealthcare, the [American health insurance system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_insurance_in_the_United_States "Health insurance in the United States"), and widespread disdain towards Thompson.[[80]](#cite_note-81)[[81]](#cite_note-82)[[82]](#cite_note-83)[[83]](#cite_note-84) Police later arrested a suspect, [Luigi Mangione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Mangione "Luigi Mangione"), and charged him with murder.[[84]](#cite_note-85) Tim Noel joined UnitedHealthcare in 2007[[85]](#cite_note-Constantino-86)[[86]](#cite_note-87)[[87]](#cite_note-88) and succeeded Brian Thompson as the CEO. Prior to becoming CEO, Noel was in charge of UnitedHealthcare's [Medicare Advantage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_Advantage "Medicare Advantage") plans.[[85]](#cite_note-Constantino-86)[[88]](#cite_note-89)[[89]](#cite_note-90)

#### Further events

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Further events")]

In November 2025, [Scott Gottlieb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Gottlieb "Scott Gottlieb"), the former [commissioner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissioner_of_Food_and_Drugs "Commissioner of Food and Drugs") of the [Food and Drug Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Drug_Administration "Food and Drug Administration"), joined UnitedHealth Group's board of directors.[[90]](#cite_note-91)

In June 2026, UnitedHealth Group announced plans to invest $3 billion in [artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence "Artificial intelligence") in 2026 and 2027.[[91]](#cite_note-92)[[92]](#cite_note-93)

## Lobbying and political activity

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Lobbying and political activity")]

In 2009, according to [OpenSecrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenSecrets "OpenSecrets"), people affiliated with UnitedHealth Group gave $4.77 million to political candidates and groups.[[117]](#cite_note-OpenSecrets-118) The [Affordable Care Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affordable_Care_Act "Affordable Care Act") was being discussed in Congress at the time and was subsequently passed in the first quarter of 2010. In 2010 UnitedHealth Group hired nine different [lobbying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lobbying "Lobbying") firms to work on its behalf.[[118]](#cite_note-119) In addition, its corporate [political action committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_action_committee "Political action committee") (PAC), called United for Health, spent an additional $1 million on lobbying activities.[[119]](#cite_note-120) UnitedHealth Group subsequently spent $4.11 million to $4.75 million from 2011 to 2021.[[117]](#cite_note-OpenSecrets-118)

### The Lewin Group

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: The Lewin Group")]

The Lewin Group is a policy research and consulting firm that provides an economic analysis of health care and human services issues and policies.[[120]](#cite_note-Becker-121) The organization has existed for about 40 years and has maintained a nonpartisan reputation through the many ownership changes that have occurred over that time.[[120]](#cite_note-Becker-121) The Lewin Group was purchased in 2007 by Ingenix, a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group, but alleges editorial and analytical "independence" from UnitedHealth Group, its parent company.[[120]](#cite_note-Becker-121) The Lewin Group discloses its ownership in its reports and on its website. While the Lewin Group does not advocate for or against any legislation, both [Democratic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)") and [Republican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republican_Party_(United_States) "Republican Party (United States)") politicians frequently cite the firm's studies to argue for and against various [U.S. healthcare reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._healthcare_reform "U.S. healthcare reform") proposals.[[121]](#cite_note-122) For example, Democratic Senator [Ron Wyden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ron_Wyden "Ron Wyden") uses Lewin Group estimates to cite the feasibility of his [Healthy Americans Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Healthy_Americans_Act "Healthy Americans Act").[[122]](#cite_note-123) Former U.S. Representative [Eric Cantor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Cantor "Eric Cantor"), the former House Republican [Whip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_whips_of_the_United_States_House_of_Representatives "Party whips of the United States House of Representatives"), has referred to the organization as "the nonpartisan Lewin Group" in arguing against government-funded health insurance proposals.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Several Lewin studies have been used to argue both for and against the inclusion of a [public option](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_health_insurance_option "Public health insurance option") in national health reform. Lewin clients who often cite its findings include [The Commonwealth Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Commonwealth_Fund "The Commonwealth Fund"), which, in 2009, held up a Lewin study it commissioned[[123]](#cite_note-124) to advocate for a public plan. The report showed that legislative proposals would achieve nearly universal coverage and "estimated that a public plan could offer small businesses insurance that is at least 9 percent cheaper than current small-business policies."[[124]](#cite_note-125)

However, the Lewin Group has acknowledged that clients sometimes choose to keep the results of studies they have commissioned private. Indeed, Lewin Group Vice President John Sheils told *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* that "sometimes studies come out that don't show exactly what the client wants to see. And in those instances, they have [the] option to bury the study."[[125]](#cite_note-126)

## Criticism and controversies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Criticism and controversies")]

|  |
| --- |
| This section needs to be **updated**. Please help update this article to reflect recent events or newly available information. *(May 2023)* |

### SEC investigation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: SEC investigation")]

In 2006, the [U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission") (SEC) began investigating the conduct of UnitedHealth Group's management and directors, for [backdating of stock options](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Options_backdating "Options backdating"). Investigations were also started by the [Internal Revenue Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revenue_Service "Internal Revenue Service") and prosecutors in the U.S. attorney's office for the Southern District of New York, who subpoenaed documents from the company. The investigations came to light after a series of probing stories in the *[Wall Street Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall_Street_Journal "Wall Street Journal")* in May 2006, discussing the apparent backdating of hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of [stock options](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_options "Stock options") by UHC management. The backdating apparently occurred with the knowledge and approval of the directors, according to the *Journal*. Major shareholders have filed lawsuits accusing former [New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey "New Jersey") governor [Thomas Kean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Kean "Thomas Kean") and UHC's other directors of failing in their fiduciary duty.[[126]](#cite_note-127) On October 15, 2006, CEO [William W. McGuire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_W._McGuire "William W. McGuire") was forced to resign, and relinquish hundreds of millions of dollars in stock options.[[127]](#cite_note-128)[[128]](#cite_note-129)[[129]](#cite_note-130)

On December 6, 2007, the SEC announced a settlement under which McGuire was to repay $468 million, including a $7 million civil penalty, as a partial settlement of the backdating prosecution. He was also barred from serving as an officer or director of a public company for ten years.[[130]](#cite_note-131)[[131]](#cite_note-132)[[132]](#cite_note-133) This was the first time in which the little-used "[clawback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clawback "Clawback")" provision under the [Sarbanes-Oxley Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarbanes-Oxley_Act "Sarbanes-Oxley Act") was used against an individual by the SEC. The SEC continued its investigations even after it in 2008 settled legal actions against both UnitedHealth Group itself and its former general counsel.[[133]](#cite_note-134)[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*]

### American Chiropractic Association lawsuit

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: American Chiropractic Association lawsuit")]

In June 2006, the [American Chiropractic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Chiropractic_Association "American Chiropractic Association") filed a national class-action lawsuit against the American Chiropractic Network (ACN), which is owned by UnitedHealth Group and administers [chiropractic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiropractic "Chiropractic") benefits, and against UnitedHealth Group itself, for alleged practices in violation of the federal [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racketeer_Influenced_and_Corrupt_Organizations_Act "Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act") (RICO).[[134]](#cite_note-135) The Missouri Department of Insurance, Financial Institutions and Professional Registration determined that UnitedHealth Group violated state insurance laws, so levied $536,000 in fines and ordered more than 50,000 cases re-opened; any improperly denied claims must have been reimbursed with interest for chiropractors and patients.[[135]](#cite_note-136)

### OptumInsight, a.k.a. Ingenix lawsuit

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: OptumInsight, a.k.a. Ingenix lawsuit")]

In February 2008, New York State Attorney General [Andrew Cuomo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cuomo "Andrew Cuomo") announced an industry-wide investigation into a scheme by health insurers to defraud consumers by manipulating reasonable and customary rates. The announcement included a statement that Cuomo intended "to file suit against Ingenix, Inc., its parent UnitedHealth Group, and three additional subsidiaries." Cuomo asserted that his investigation found that rates found in a database of health care charges maintained by Ingenix were lower than what he determined was the actual cost of certain medical expenses. Cuomo said this inappropriately allowed health insurance companies to deny a portion of provider claims, thereby pushing costs down to members.[[136]](#cite_note-137)

On January 13, 2009, Ingenix announced an agreement with the New York State attorney settling the probe into the independence of the health pricing database. Under the settlement, UnitedHealth Group and Ingenix would pay $50 million to finance a new, non-profit entity that would develop a new healthcare pricing database. Ingenix would discontinue its medical pricing databases when the new entity makes its product available. The company acknowledged the appearance of a conflict of interest but admitted no wrongdoing.[[137]](#cite_note-138)

On January 15, 2009, UnitedHealth Group announced a $350 million settlement of three class action lawsuits filed in Federal court by the [American Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Medical_Association "American Medical Association"), UnitedHealth Group members, healthcare providers, and state medical societies for not paying out-of-network benefits. This settlement came two days after a similar settlement with Cuomo.[[138]](#cite_note-139)[[139]](#cite_note-140)

On October 27, 2009, Cuomo announced the creation of [FAIR Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FAIR_Health?action=edit&redlink=1 "FAIR Health (page does not exist)"), an independent, non-profit organization that would develop a nationwide database for consumer reimbursement, as well as a website where consumers would be able to compare prices before choosing doctors. To fund FAIR Health, the Attorney General's office secured nearly $100 million from insurers such as [Aetna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aetna "Aetna"), UnitedHealth Group, and [Anthem Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthem_Inc. "Anthem Inc.")[[140]](#cite_note-141)

### PacifiCare fine in California

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: PacifiCare fine in California")]

In 2008, the [California Department of Insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_Department_of_Insurance "California Department of Insurance") took action against UnitedHealthcare's subsidiary [PacifiCare Health Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PacifiCare_Health_Systems "PacifiCare Health Systems"), acquired in 2005, ultimately fining UnitedHealthcare around $173 million for an estimated over 900,000 violations of the Unfair Insurance Practices Act; by 2019, the case was still being disputed in court, with the possibility of affirming $91 million in penalties.[[141]](#cite_note-142)[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*]

### Medicare overbilling lawsuit

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Medicare overbilling lawsuit")]

A [whistleblower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whistleblower "Whistleblower") lawsuit filed in 2011 charged UnitedHealth Group's data analytics division with assisting in defrauding [Medicare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_(United_States) "Medicare (United States)") by boosting risk adjustment scores from [Medicare Advantage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_Advantage "Medicare Advantage") companies. The suit alleged that UnitedHealth Group subsidiary Ingenix (now OptumInsight) "defrauded the United States of hundreds of millions – and likely billions – of dollars." Former UnitedHealth executive Benjamin Poehling brought the suit under the [False Claims Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_Claims_Act "False Claims Act"). The government said it would proceed on claims against two healthcare companies, UnitedHealth and its Texas subsidiary WellMed Medical Management. In February 2017, a federal judge unsealed the suit after the [Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") announced it would join the case.[[142]](#cite_note-143)[[143]](#cite_note-144)[*[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")*]

### CMS fine over Medicare Part D

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=UnitedHealth_Group&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: CMS fine over Medicare Part D")]

In 2017, the [Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centers_for_Medicare_and_Medicaid_Services "Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services") (CMS) fined UnitedHealthcare $2.5 million after discovering issues in [Medicare Part D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medicare_Part_D "Medicare Part D") leading to delays or denials in a 2016 audit.[[144]](#cite_note-145)

### 2018 New Jersey fine

# UnitedHealth Group - Wikipedia Summary

**UnitedHealth Group Incorporated** is an American multinational for-profit healthcare company headquartered in Eden Prairie, Minnesota, specializing in health insurance and healthcare services. It is the world's fourth-largest company by revenue and the largest healthcare company by revenue, ranked fourth on the 2026 Fortune Global 500. The company has a market capitalization of over $400 billion and insures over 50 million people in the United States.

## Key Financial Data (2025)
- Revenue: $447.6 billion
- Net income: $12.81 billion
- Total assets: $309.6 billion
- Employees: ~390,000

## History
Founded in 1974 as CharterMed by Richard T. Burke, it became UnitedHealthcare Corporation in 1977 and went public in 1984. The company rebranded as UnitedHealth Group in 1998. Major acquisitions include MetraHealth (1995), Oxford Health Plans (2004), PacifiCare Health Systems (2005), and Change Healthcare (2021, completed 2022).

## Organizational Structure
The company operates through two main subsidiaries:
- **Optum** (formed 2011) - provides data/analytics, pharmacy care, population health, healthcare delivery, and operations
- **UnitedHealthcare** - insurance and managed care division

## 2024 Events
- **Killing of Brian Thompson** (Dec 4, 2024): CEO of UnitedHealthcare subsidiary was shot and killed in NYC outside the New York Hilton Midtown. Suspect Luigi Mangione was arrested and charged with murder. Reactions on social media showed widespread resentment toward UnitedHealthcare and the American health insurance system. Tim Noel succeeded Thompson as CEO.
- **Change Healthcare ransomware attack** (Feb 2024): The subsidiary was crippled by a ransomware attack. CEO Andrew Witty testified before the US House and Senate about the cyberattack.

## 2026 Developments
- Scott Gottlieb, former FDA commissioner, joined the board of directors (Nov 2025)
- UnitedHealth Group announced $3 billion investment in AI for 2026-2027 (June 2026)

## Controversies and Legal Issues
UnitedHealth Group has faced numerous investigations, lawsuits, and fines including:
- **SEC investigation** (2006): Stock option backdating scandal leading to CEO William McGuire's resignation and $468 million repayment
- **Ingenix lawsuit** (2008-2009): NY Attorney General investigation into manipulated healthcare pricing databases; $350 million settlement
- **Medicare overbilling lawsuit** (2011): Whistleblower case alleging defrauding Medicare via risk adjustment scores
- **Use of AI to deny claims**: Algorithmic model used to deny healthcare claims
- **PacifiCare fine**: ~$173 million fine by California Department of Insurance
- Multiple other lawsuits regarding Medicare Advantage overbilling, mental health treatment denials, anticompetitive behavior, and more

## Lobbying
The company spent $4.11-$4.77 million annually on lobbying activities from 2009-2021. Its subsidiary, The Lewin Group, is a policy research firm that maintains editorial independence from its parent company.

# UnitedHealth Group

UnitedHealth Group is the largest healthcare provider in the United States, holding over 15.3% of the health insurance market as of 2021. Founded in 1974 as Charter Med Incorporated, it underwent several transformations and restructuring, ultimately rebranding itself to UnitedHealth Group to encompass a diverse range of subsidiary businesses. The organization is primarily divided into two divisions: UnitedHealthcare, which manages health insurance plans for millions domestically and internationally, and Optum, which focuses on healthcare services like medical research, pharmacy care, and technological development in health facilities.

Throughout its history, UnitedHealth Group has been involved in significant acquisitions and expansions, including its notable partnership with AARP and its strategic decision to exit most Affordable Care Act state exchanges in 2016 due to financial losses. However, in 2021, the company announced its re-entry into several state markets, aiming to address the growing demand for affordable healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic. UnitedHealth Group has faced controversies as well, particularly regarding allegations of overbilling in Medicare, which it has denied, asserting that the claims are based on outdated data. As of 2023, the company continues to expand its services, providing coverage for a substantial portion of Medicare recipients and reporting significant profits.

## Full Article

### Company information

* **Date founded:** 1974
* **Industry:** Healthcare
* **Corporate headquarters:** Minnetonka, MN
* **Type:** Public

### Overview

*UnitedHealth Group* is the largest healthcare company in the United States by revenue. It had captured more than 14 percent of the American health insurance market. The organization was founded as Charter Med Incorporated in 1974 and later renamed UnitedHealth Group to reflect its growing brand and several subsidiary businesses.

UnitedHealth Group’s subsidiary businesses each cater to specific parts of the [healthcare industry](/research-starters/health-and-medicine/medicine-and-health-care-industry). These subsidiaries are primarily part of two of the company’s divisions: UnitedHealthcare and Optum. UnitedHealthcare and its subsidiaries manage millions of healthcare plans across America and millions more abroad. Optum and its subsidiaries are responsible for medical research, filling prescriptions, and the development of medical facilities and technologies.

UnitedHealth Group has made national headlines on several occasions. In 2016, it announced that it would be leaving most of the state markets created by the [Affordable Care Act](/research-starters/consumer-health/patient-protection-and-affordable-care-act-overview), legislation intended to reduce the price of health insurance for individuals. UnitedHealth Group explained that it had taken significant losses in these state markets and considered them volatile. However, in 2021, UnitedHealth Group announced an expansion of its services to seven state markets in an attempt to profit from market changes caused by COVID-19.

UnitedHealth Group has had its share of controversies. In 2021, federal regulatory agencies alleged that it had collected far more in risk-adjusted [Medicare](/research-starters/consumer-health/medicare) payments than any other company. The regulatory agencies were concerned that such a discrepancy was caused by intentional manipulation of data to collect inappropriate payments and maximize profits. UnitedHealth Group denied these allegations, arguing that the findings were based on out-of-date and inaccurate data.

### History

UnitedHealth Group was originally founded in 1974 by Richard Taylor Burke as Charter Med Incorporated. At the time, the organization was structured as a privately held company. In 1977, Charter Med Incorporated underwent significant restructuring, emerging as United Healthcare Corporation. Though Charter Med Incorporated continued to exist, United Healthcare Corporation became its parent company.

United Healthcare Corporation launched Diversified Pharmaceutical Services, a pharmacy benefit management subsidiary, in 1988. However, Diversified Pharmaceutical Services did not remain with United Healthcare Corporation and was instead sold to SmithKline Beecham in 1994. That same year, United Healthcare acquired the health insurance company Ramsey-HMO.

Though the company grew through aggressive [acquisitions](/research-starters/business-and-management/business-acquisitions), it did not achieve its first major success until 1997, when United Healthcare Corporation was selected to provide insurance coverage for the AARP (formerly known as the [American Association of Retired Persons](/research-starters/political-science/american-association-retired-persons-aarp)). That same year, the company significantly expanded its Evercare program, a health management program specifically tailored to provide long-term care to older adult patients in assisted living facilities and nursing homes. Unlike traditional healthcare plans, Evercare offered special coverage for people suffering from chronic illnesses and individuals whose health limited them to the confines of their homes.

Because of its acquisitions, in 1998, United Healthcare Corporation underwent another significant restructuring. It became a subsidiary of the larger UnitedHealth Group, which also managed Uniprise, Ovations, and numerous other healthcare providers. UnitedHealth Group then purchased AmeriChoice and GeoAccess in 2002 and Mid Atlantic Medical Services in 2003. These acquisitions allowed UnitedHealth Group to expand its services and enter new markets.

UnitedHealth Group continued acquiring health insurance providers across the country. Some of these acquisitions, such as John Deere Health Care Inc., were specialized healthcare services tailored for specific markets. John Deere Health Care was available to John Deere employees. Others, such as PacifiCare Health Systems, were larger networks that provided a wide variety of services to patients. In 2011, UnitedHealth Group created Optum, a brand dedicated specifically to healthcare services. Other more specialized variants of Optum were later created by UnitedHealth Group, such as Optum Rx and Optum Bank.

In 2016, UnitedHealth Group announced that it planned to exit most of the Affordable Care Act state exchanges. At the time, UnitedHealth Group was the largest health insurer in the United States, so the announcement generated significant media attention. Stephen Hemsley, CEO of UnitedHealth Group, noted that the exchanges were too small and risky to be profitable. Hemsley also stated that at the time of his remarks, UnitedHealth Group had lost roughly $475 million in Affordable Care Act exchanges in the previous year and was on track to lose roughly $500 million that year. Though the company planned to pull out from the state market exchanges, Hemsley noted that UnitedHealth Group would continue to advocate for innovative and sustainable approaches that better served the people who rely on the national healthcare market.

At the time, experts noted that UnitedHealth Group’s departure from the Affordable Care Act would likely result in increased premiums for healthcare purchasers and additional scrutiny of the Affordable Care Act legislation, which was intended to reduce healthcare costs for Americans. However, when asked for a comment, representatives from UnitedHealth Group noted that the health insurance industry was growing, and such programs were clearly desired by consumers. Because of this, representatives from UnitedHealth Group recommended that observers not judge the success of the marketplaces created by the Affordable Care Act on the actions of a single business but rather on how it benefited Americans.

Following its announcement that it would soon exit state marketplaces, UnitedHealth Group announced its plans to acquire several other companies, increasing its share of the health insurance marketplace. In 2017, the company acquired Rally Health, with which it had previously been involved as an investor. It later acquired both DaVita Medical Group and Equian.

In 2020 and 2021, the COVID-19 pandemic placed significant strains on the US healthcare system. Data showed that these pressing circumstances increased the number of Americans who were unable to afford their rising healthcare premiums. These difficulties caused more people to participate in the state markets created by the Affordable Care Act. To capitalize on these increasingly profitable markets, UnitedHealth Group announced that it would reconsider its plans to leave most state markets. In 2021, the company announced that it would expand its health insurance products into seven states. UnitedHealth Group planned to sell insurance for both individuals and families in these markets, which included Florida, Georgia, Michigan, Texas, Illinois, Alabama, and Louisiana. The policies went into effect in 2022, and UnitedHealth Group hoped that this venture into the state markets would be more profitable than its last. In 2023, UnitedHealth Group announced it was further expanding its services to make its plans available to 95 percent of Medicare beneficiaries in the United States, securing its position as the nation’s leading Medicare provider. UnitedHealth Group reported strong growth in 2023, with the company reporting $5.6 billion in profits in the first quarter of the year.

In 2024, the UnitedHealth subsidiary Change Healthcare experienced a cyberattack that disrupted insurance payments and compromised the personal information of more than 100 million individuals, making it one of the largest healthcare data breaches in US history. On December 4, 2024, Brian Thompson, the CEO of UnitedHealth's insurance division, was shot and killed in New York City. This incident brought significant attention to the company and the broader health insurance industry. Tim Noel, a company veteran, was appointed as the CEO of UnitedHealthcare in January 2025. Also in early 2025, the Justice Department and attorneys general from four states filed a lawsuit to block UnitedHealth's $3.3 billion acquisition of Amedisys, arguing that the merger would reduce competition in the home health and hospice care markets.

### Impact

UnitedHealth Group is divided into two brands, with each providing different services to the marketplace. UnitedHealthcare directly provides health insurance plans to consumers. ### History

UnitedHealth Group was originally founded in 1974 by Richard Taylor Burke as Charter Med Incorporated. At the time, the organization was structured as a privately held company. Though Charter Med Incorporated continued to exist, United Healthcare Corporation became its parent company.

United Healthcare Corporation launched Diversified Pharmaceutical Services, a pharmacy benefit management subsidiary, in 1988. That same year, United Healthcare acquired the health insurance company Ramsey-HMO.

Though the company grew through aggressive [acquisitions](/research-starters/business-and-management/business-acquisitions), it did not achieve its first major success until 1997, when United Healthcare Corporation was selected to provide insurance coverage for the AARP (formerly known as the [American Association of Retired Persons](/research-starters/political-science/american-association-retired-persons-aarp)). Unlike traditional healthcare plans, Evercare offered special coverage for people suffering from chronic illnesses and individuals whose health limited them to the confines of their homes.

Because of its acquisitions, in 1998, United Healthcare Corporation underwent another significant restructuring. It became a subsidiary of the larger UnitedHealth Group, which also managed Uniprise, Ovations, and numerous other healthcare providers. Though the company planned to pull out from the state market exchanges, Hemsley noted that UnitedHealth Group would continue to advocate for innovative and sustainable approaches that better served the people who rely on the national healthcare market.

# UnitedHealth Group

![Portrait of Gail Boudreaux wearing a dark blazer and pearl earrings, looking slightly to the side against a dark background.](https://cdn.britannica.com/12/278412-050-8F580324/Portrait-of-Gail-Boudreaux.jpg?c=crop&h=40&w=50)
![Aerial view of Eli Lilly and Company's Indianapolis headquarters.](https://cdn.britannica.com/64/256064-050-F91AE7DC/aerial-headquarters-Eli-Lilly-Indianapolis.jpg?c=crop&h=40&w=50)
![A selection of pharmaceuticals](https://cdn.britannica.com/22/156622-050-0A33671D/assorted-pills-medicine.jpg?c=crop&h=40&w=50)
![UnitedHealthcare headquarters in Minnetonka, Minnesota, USA, May 5, 2023. ](https://cdn.britannica.com/56/275156-050-29850A12/united-health-care-headquarters-minnetonka-minnesota.jpg?w=385)

UnitedHealth Group is the largest [health insurance](/money/health-insurance) provider in the United States, serving more than 29 million Americans, and more than 50 million people worldwide. Since its inception in the 1970s, the company has grown steadily through acquisitions, a strategy that has at times drawn antitrust scrutiny. As of 2025, UnitedHealth Group ranked third on the [Fortune 500](/topic/Fortune-500) list, behind only **[Walmart](/money/Walmart)** (WMT) and **[Amazon](/money/Amazoncom)** (AMZN).

## Business model

UnitedHealth Group is split into two divisions: **UnitedHealthcare**, which provides insurance plans, and **Optum**, its noninsurance medical services group. UnitedHealthcare, which accounts for over half of the company’s revenue, is divided into four segments:

Optum, which was created in 2011, provides medical services outside of insurance. It is divided into three segments:

## 1970s–2000: HMO innovation and early growth

UnitedHealth was founded by Richard Taylor Burke as **Charter Med Incorporated** in 1974 and restructured as **United Healthcare Corporation** in 1977. The company initially focused on [health maintenance organizations](/topic/health-maintenance-organization) (HMOs), a novel concept at the time, that prioritized preventative care and paid doctors for the number of patients seen rather than services provided. By 1984, the company operated 11 HMOs across 10 states; it purchased HMOs Share Development and Peak Health Care over the next two years. Kennett Simmons, the former president of Peak Health Care, took over the company after Burke resigned after a conflict over coverage with member hospitals.

The company went public in 1984 and began expanding through acquisitions the following decade, beginning with its acquisition of Ramsey-HMO in 1994. Revenue climbed past $11 billion by 1997, reflecting the company’s rapid expansion. The same year, it was chosen as the insurance provider for the [American Association of Retired Persons](/topic/American-Association-of-Retired-Persons) (AARP). The company was restructured again in 1998, with United Healthcare Corp. becoming a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group.

## 2000–2010: Aggressive expansion and legal woes

In 2000 the American Medical Association brought a class-action lawsuit alleging that UnitedHealth used faulty data in order to reduce payouts to physicians and plan members. (UnitedHealth settled the lawsuit in 2009 for $350 billion without admitting or denying guilt.)

In 2002 UnitedHealth expanded its Medicaid services by acquiring AmeriChoice for $530 million. The company continued its vigorous acquisition strategy into the early to mid-2000s, acquiring companies including Mid Atlantic Medical (in a $2.7 billion deal), Oxford Health ($4.9 billion), and PacifiCare ($8.1 billion). In 2006 the company was involved in a scandal when then-CEO William McGuire was found to have been backdating [stock options](/money/what-are-incentive-stock-options) as a result of a [U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission](/money/Securities-and-Exchange-Commission) investigation. McGuire quickly stepped down.

In 2007 the company announced a deal to acquire Nevada-based Sierra Health Services. The [Department of Justice](/topic/US-Department-of-Justice) sued UnitedHealth Group to stop the merger, fearing the acquisition would reduce Medicare service competition in the state. The deal went through the following year after UnitedHealth agreed to sell its Las Vegas [Medicare Advantage](/money/what-is-medicare-advantage-part-c) program to competitor **Humana** (HUM).

## 2010–2020: Entering Optum and exiting the Affordable Care Act

In 2011 UnitedHealth unified its health services under the Optum brand. Alongside the already existing Optum Health, the company’s Ingenix brand was renamed Optum Insight and its Prescription Solutions brand was renamed Optum Rx. The company continued to invest into the health services side of its business when it acquired Catamaran in 2015, which at the time processed the fourth-largest number of prescriptions in the U.S., in a deal valued at just under $13 billion.

In 2016 UnitedHealth Group announced it would be exiting all but a few [Affordable Care Act](/money/Patient-Protection-and-Affordable-Care-Act) state exchanges, citing hundreds of millions of dollars in losses in 2015 and 2016. However, the company would reenter the marketplace in several states by the early 2020s.

![Stephen Hemsley, president and CEO of the UnitedHealth Group, speaks during a joint press conference with Cisco announcing their Connected Care initiative on Capitol Hill in Washington on July 15, 2009.](https://cdn.britannica.com/57/275157-050-354801FB/president-and-ceo-of-unitedhealth-group-stephen-hemsley.jpg?w=385)

The company continued to build out its health services portfolio with the 2017 acquisition of Surgical Care Associates, which operated around 200 surgery centers. In 2019, it bought DaVita medical group, adding another 280 clinics and 35 urgent care centers to its portfolio.

## 2020s: Antitrust wins, Medicare controversies, and executive shake-ups

UnitedHealth Group faced significant controversy for its interactions with Medicare Advantage during the early to mid-2020s, with the Department of Justice filing a lawsuit alleging that the company “obtained inflated risk adjustment payments based on untruthful and inaccurate information about the health status of beneficiaries.” Although the case was initially brought forward by a whistleblower in 2011 before being taken over by the Department of Justice in 2017, investigations into the scandal by outlets including *[The New York Times](/topic/The-New-York-Times)*, [The Wall Street Journal](/topic/The-Wall-Street-Journal), and [The Guardian](/topic/The-Guardian-British-newspaper) added new layers and fuel to the controversy.

In 2023 the company secured its largest acquisition since Catamaran when it acquired medical payment-processing firm Change Healthcare in a $13 billion deal, despite a challenge from the Department of Justice.

In December 2024, UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson was shot and killed in New York City. [Luigi Mangione](/biography/Luigi-Mangione) was later arrested and charged with the crime. The shooting sparked intense media coverage, with some online communities portraying Mangione as a symbol of resistance against the health insurance industry.

Just days after the shooting, UnitedHealth Group CEO Andrew Witty published an op-ed in the *New York Times* titled “The Health Care System Is Flawed. Let’s Fix It.” Witty abruptly stepped down in May 2025, citing personal reasons—although the exit closely followed the company reporting an earnings miss for the first time since 2008. Witty was replaced by Stephen Hemsley, the company’s executive chairman, who had previously served as CEO from 2006–2017.

## UnitedHealth legacy

Over five decades, UnitedHealth Group has evolved from a regional HMO innovator into a global health care powerhouse. Its dual-engine model—combining insurance with expansive medical services through Optum—has helped reshape how care is delivered and paid for in the U.S. health system. Although its acquisition-driven growth has drawn scrutiny and sparked legal challenges, UnitedHealth’s scale, influence, and profitability have made it a defining force in modern American health care—and a benchmark for the scale and complexity of today’s system.

args.summary:
UnitedHealth Group is the largest health insurance provider in the United States, serving over 29 million Americans and more than 50 million people worldwide. As of 2025, it ranked third on the Fortune 500 behind Walmart and Amazon. The company operates through two divisions: UnitedHealthcare (insurance plans, over half of revenue) and Optum (noninsurance medical services, created in 2011).

Founded in 1974 as Charter Med Incorporated by Richard Taylor Burke, the company initially focused on HMOs. It went public in 1984 and expanded through acquisitions, including Ramsey-HMO (1994), AmeriChoice (2002), Mid Atlantic Medical ($2.7B), Oxford Health ($4.9B), and PacifiCare ($8.1B). In 2006, CEO William McGuire resigned after a stock options backdating scandal.

In 2011, the company unified its health services under the Optum brand. It acquired Catamaran (2015, ~$13B), Surgical Care Associates (2017), and DaVita medical group (2019). The company exited most Affordable Care Act exchanges in 2016 but reentered by the early 2020s.

In the 2020s, the company faced Department of Justice scrutiny over Medicare Advantage risk adjustment payments. In 2023, it acquired Change Healthcare for $13B. In December 2024, UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson was shot and killed in New York City; Luigi Mangione was charged. CEO Andrew Witty stepped down in May 2025, replaced by Stephen Hemsley (former CEO 2006–2017).

**Ping An Insurance** known also as **Ping An of China** ([simplified Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simplified_Chinese_characters "Simplified Chinese characters"): 中国平安; [traditional Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_Chinese_characters "Traditional Chinese characters"): 中國平安; [pinyin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinyin "Pinyin"): *Zhōngguó Píng Ān*), full name **Ping An Insurance (Group) Company of China, Ltd.** is a Chinese [financial services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_services "Financial services") [holding company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_company "Holding company") whose subsidiaries provide [insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance "Insurance"), [banking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banking "Banking"), [asset management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asset_management "Asset management"), [financial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_services "Financial services") services. The company was founded in 1988 and is headquartered in [Shenzhen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhen "Shenzhen"). "Ping An" literally means "safe and well".

In 2024, Ping An ranked 29th on the Forbes Global 2000 list and 53rd on the [Fortune Global 500](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortune_Global_500 "Fortune Global 500") list.[[3]](#cite_note-3) Ping An has been ranked by Brand Finance as the world's most valuable insurance brand for six years running.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Ping An Insurance is one of the top 50 companies in the Shanghai Stock Exchange. It is also a constituent stock of Hang Seng Index, an index of the top companies in the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. Ping An Insurance was also included in the pan-China stock indices CSI 300 Index,[[5]](#cite_note-5) FTSE China A50 Index[[6]](#cite_note-6) and Hang Seng China 50 Index.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

## Business

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ping_An_Insurance&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Business")]

**Ping An Insurance Group** started off in 1988 as a property and casualty insurance company, later diversifying into insurance, banking, asset management, financial services and healthcare services.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Ping An has licenses to offer financial services, including insurance, banking, trusts, securities, futures and financial leasing.[[9]](#cite_note-9)

Ping An has also adopted an integrated financial model on a mix of business lines, including life insurance, P&C insurance, banking and securities.[[10]](#cite_note-10) The company invests 1% of its revenues into R&D each year to branch out its businesses, adopt technology and support the building of its healthcare and senior care ecosystem.[[11]](#cite_note-11)

Since the mid-1990s, Ping An has been subsequently taken investments from overseas firms such as [Morgan Stanley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Stanley "Morgan Stanley") and [Goldman Sachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldman_Sachs "Goldman Sachs") in 1994. In 2002 [HSBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSBC "HSBC") took a large equity interest in Ping An.[[12]](#cite_note-12) In early 2008, Ping An agreed to take a 50% share in Fortis Investments, a subsidiary of [Fortis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortis_(finance) "Fortis (finance)"),[[13]](#cite_note-13) which had taken over ABN AMRO Asset Management as a result of the split up of [ABN AMRO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABN_AMRO "ABN AMRO") in late 2007; the deal was canceled in October 2008.[[14]](#cite_note-14)

In June 2009, Ping An became a strategic investor in [Shenzhen Development Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shenzhen_Development_Bank "Shenzhen Development Bank")[[15]](#cite_note-15) (now part of [Ping An Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ping_An_Bank "Ping An Bank")).

In 2012, the company created Ping An Ventures, a $150M VC fund which invested in over 100 companies, such as [Didi Chuxing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Didi_Chuxing "Didi Chuxing"), [Hycor Biomedical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hycor_Biomedical "Hycor Biomedical"), [Meituan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meituan "Meituan"), [Oscar Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Health "Oscar Health"), [Payoneer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payoneer "Payoneer"), [Taulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taulia_(company) "Taulia (company)"), and others.[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17) In 2014, together with SBT Venture Capital Ping An led a $27M funding round for [eToro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EToro "EToro").[[18]](#cite_note-18)

In 2016, Ping An Healthcare and Technology (Ping An Good Doctor) completed a Series A funding round of a total of US$500 million, making its valuation hit US$3 billion. Ping An also bought a 48% stake in Chinese car website Autohome Inc. from Telstra Corp. for $1.6 billion.[[19]](#cite_note-19)

In February 2018, three technology subsidiaries of Ping An completed private placement financing, which received positive responses particularly from international institutional investors. They were Ping An Healthcare and Technology Company Limited, Ping An Medical and Healthcare Management Co., Ltd and [OneConnect Financial Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OneConnect_Financial_Technology "OneConnect Financial Technology") Co., LTD.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

In June 2019, Ping An One Connect Bank officially commenced operation after receiving a virtual banking license from the [Hong Kong Monetary Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hong_Kong_Monetary_Authority "Hong Kong Monetary Authority") in May 2019. In December 2019, OneConnect Financial Technology was listed on the New York Stock Exchange.[[21]](#cite_note-21)

In 2019, Ping An became the first insurance company from mainland China to be selected for the Dow Jones Sustainability Emerging Markets Index (DJSI).[[22]](#cite_note-22)

In October 2020, [Lufax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lufax "Lufax"), one of China's leading online wealth management platform, listed on the New York Stock Exchange.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

In May 2021, Ping An released the Ping An Zhen Yi Nian healthcare brand. The product line was mainly targeted at supporting urban elderly care communities, and integrates corporate finance, medical care and health technology.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

In July 2021, Ping An and Shionogi signed agreements to launch joint ventures in Shanghai and Hong Kong. Ping An-Shionogi is a Healthcare as a Service (HaaS) enterprise, an integrated medical and healthcare platform for public health and patients. The joint venture is a collaboration between the Ping An and Shionogi on drug research, development, production and sales.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

In October 2021, Ping An Bank rolled out services under the Cross-boundary Wealth Management Connect pilot scheme.[[26]](#cite_note-26)

In January 2022, Ping An Life (a subsidiary of Ping An) received approval from the CBIRC for its investment in New Founder Group.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In July 2022, OneConnect (Ping An's fintech subsidiary) listed on the main board of the Hong Kong Stock Exchange by way of introduction and dual-primary listing.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

In February 2023, Ping An Bank Hong Kong Branch was granted an insurance agency license by the Hong Kong [Insurance Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance_Authority "Insurance Authority").[[29]](#cite_note-29)

In November 2023, it was entered into the [MSCI KLD 400 Social Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSCI_KLD_400_Social_Index "MSCI KLD 400 Social Index").[[30]](#cite_note-30)

As of 30 June 2024, Ping An has grown its health ecosystem in China by partnering with the country's top 100 hospitals and 3A hospitals, 50,000 in-house and contracted external doctors and 233,000 pharmacies.[[31]](#cite_note-31) Ping An's home-based senior care services covered 64 cities across China with over 120,000 customers entitled to the benefits.[[32]](#cite_note-32) Customer's entitled to service benefits in the healthcare and elderlycare ecosystem accounted for over 68% of Ping An Life's new business value in 2024.[[33]](#cite_note-33)

In February 2025, Ping An Healthcare and Technology announced that its artificial intelligence model and its platform designed for doctors now have built in access to DeepSeek's model. Ping An said access to DeepSeek's model will help to further enhance its medical services by assisting doctors in making more accurate diagnoses and providing personalized health management. Ping An Healthcare and Technology is undergoing further research and development of AI technology.[[34]](#cite_note-34)

## Ownership

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ping_An_Insurance&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Ownership")]

Ping An is a publicly listed company.[[35]](#cite_note-35)

As of 30 June 2024, CP Group Ltd. indirectly held 964,427,077 H shares of the Company, representing approximately 5.30% of the total share capital of the Company.

Ping An has the classification of a [civilian-run enterprise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilian-run_enterprise "Civilian-run enterprise"). [Richard McGregor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_McGregor "Richard McGregor"), author of *[The Party: The Secret World of China's Communist Rulers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Party:_The_Secret_World_of_China's_Communist_Rulers "The Party: The Secret World of China's Communist Rulers")*,[[36]](#cite_note-36) said that "the true ownership of large chunks of its shares remains unclear" and that the ownership of Ping An is a "murky structure".[[37]](#cite_note-McGregor204205-37) In October 2012, *[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* reported that relatives and associates of Chinese [Premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Premier of the People's Republic of China") [Wen Jiabao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wen_Jiabao "Wen Jiabao") controlled stakes in Ping An worth at least US$2.2 billion in 2007.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

## Markets

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ping_An_Insurance&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Markets")]

Since 24 June 2004 Ping An has been listed on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (subsidiary of Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing) as SEHK: 2318. Since 1 March 2007, it has a listing on the Shanghai Stock Exchange as SSE: 601318. Since 19 June 2023, its yuan-denominated shares has a listing on the Stock Exchange of Hong Kong as SEHK: 82318.

Ping An replaced Anhui Expressway in the [Hang Seng China Enterprises Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hang_Seng_China_Enterprises_Index "Hang Seng China Enterprises Index") (HSCEI) in 2004.[[39]](#cite_note-39)

The Hang Seng Index Services Company announced on 11 May 2007, that Ping An would join as [Hang Seng Index Constituent Stock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hang_Seng_Index "Hang Seng Index") effective on 4 June 2007.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

## Operations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ping_An_Insurance&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Operations")]

Ping An has operations across all of mainland China, and in Hong Kong and Macau through Ping An Insurance Overseas. Lufax, OneConnect and Ping An Good Doctor have now expanded overseas. OneConnect serves 100+ customers in 20 countries and regions mainly in Southeast Asia.

args.summary:
Ping An Insurance (also known as Ping An of China) is a Chinese financial services holding company headquartered in Shenzhen, founded in 1988 by Ma Mingzhe. It provides insurance, banking, asset management, and healthcare services. In 2024, it ranked 29th on the Forbes Global 2000 and 53rd on the Fortune Global 500, and has been named the world's most valuable insurance brand by Brand Finance for six consecutive years. The company is publicly listed on both the Shanghai Stock Exchange (SSE: 601318) and Hong Kong Stock Exchange (SEHK: 2318, 82318), and is a constituent of the Hang Seng Index and CSI 300 Index.

Key financials for 2024: Revenue CN¥1,141,346M, net income CN¥126,607M, total assets CN¥12,957,827M, with approximately 273,053 employees.

The company started as a property and casualty insurer and diversified into life insurance, health insurance, banking, asset management, and healthcare. It has invested in technology and R&D (1% of revenues), and notable subsidiaries include Ping An Bank, Ping An Good Doctor (healthcare), OneConnect (fintech), and Lufax (wealth management). Major historical events include investments from Morgan Stanley/Goldman Sachs (1994), HSBC (2002), a failed Fortis deal (2008), strategic investment in Shenzhen Development Bank (2009), and creation of Ping An Ventures ($150M VC fund). In 2025, Ping An Healthcare integrated DeepSeek's AI model to enhance medical services.

Ownership: CP Group Ltd. holds 5.30% as of June 2024. The company is classified as a civilian-run enterprise, though its ownership structure has been described as "murky" by journalist Richard McGregor, with a 2012 NYT report alleging relatives of Premier Wen Jiabao controlled stakes worth over $2.2 billion.
