## Our History

Berkshire Hathaway Homestate Companies (BHHC) began as eight separately managed regional insurance companies across the United States.

As originally chartered, each wrote primarily in its own “home state” – with some business in bordering states. The eight companies began as personal lines writers, and each had its local underwriting and management presence in their territories – a core strategy BHHC continues to embody.

### Highlights

#### How It All Started

* Founded more than 50 years ago, Berkshire Hathaway Homestate Companies (BHHC) began as eight separately managed regional insurance companies located across the United States.
* As originally chartered, each company wrote primarily in its own “home state” – with some business in bordering states. The eight companies began as personal lines writers.
* Each company had its own local underwriting and management presence in its respective territories – a core value BHHC continues to embody.
* Starting in the late 1990s, the remaining six companies began operating under the shared brand identity of Berkshire Hathaway Homestate Companies. The name was selected as a legacy to its local roots, while also representing the superior financial strength associated with being a Berkshire Hathaway company.

Today, BHHC has expanded its footprint nationally, while remaining committed to our heritage of offering the personalized service of a local home state insurance company. Our local presence, combined with our unparalleled financial strength, has resulted in knowledge, experience and staying power, allowing us to provide you solid and secure insurance products.

### Berkshire Hathaway Homestate Companies

##### Berkshire Hathaway Homestate Insurance Company

Berkshire Hathaway Homestate Insurance Company is an Omaha, Nebraska domiciled company. It was originally incorporated as Cornhusker Casualty Company in 1970 writing business in the state of Nebraska. In 1981, the Company acquired the Insurance Company of Iowa – an affiliated Iowa-domiciled insurance company.

In 2012, in response to its growing national presence, the company changed its name to Berkshire Hathaway Homestate Insurance Company to better reflect its current national market position.

##### BHHC Special Risks Insurance Company

BHHC Special Risks Insurance Company is a North Liberty, Iowa domiciled surplus lines insurer. It was originally incorporated as Brookwood Insurance Company and began writing business in 1999. It historically focused its business within Oregon and Tennessee. In 2021, the company changed its name to BHHC Special Risks Insurance Company.

##### Continental Divide Insurance Company

Continental Divide Insurance Company is a Denver, Colorado domiciled company. The company was incorporated in 1978 to write business in the state of Colorado.

##### Cypress Insurance Company

Cypress Insurance Company is a San Francisco, California domiciled company. The company began writing business in 1963 and was acquired by Berkshire Hathaway in 1977. Cypress Insurance Company serves as our leading writer for workers compensation insurance in California.

##### Oak River Insurance Company

Oak River Insurance Company is an Omaha, Nebraska domiciled company. The company began writing business in 1993 and, in the same year, merged with Kansas Fire & Casualty Insurance Company. The combined companies continued on under the Oak River Insurance Company name.

##### Redwood Fire and Casualty Insurance Company

Redwood Fire and Casualty Insurance Company is an Omaha, Nebraska domiciled company. Originally incorporated as Kerkling Reinsurance Corporation in 1970, it was acquired by Berkshire Hathaway in 1976. The company changed its name to Central Fire & Casualty Company in 1977 and then assumed its current name in 1980.

Contents

![Hathaway](http://www.omahaimc.org/wp-content/uploads/Hathaway.jpg)According to the Forbes Global 2000 list and formula, Berkshire Hathaway is the third largest public company in the world. By revenue, it is the 9th largest conglomerate. It is also the largest financial service company by revenue.

Listed on the New York Stock Exchange, it is famous for having the most expensive share price in history. At the time of writing, a Class A share in Berkshire Hathaway Inc. cost 312,850 USD. The company chairman Warren Buffett has declared that there will not be a stock split, since he believes that a high share price attracts investors that are focused on long-term profits rather than short-term price fluctuations.

* Dairy Queen

* Fruit of the Loom

Examples of companies where Berkshire Hathaway owns part of the company are Pilot Flying, United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, Southwest Airlines, American Airlines, Kraft Heinz Company, American Express, Wells Fargo, The Coca-Cola Company, Bank of America, and Apple.

Warren Buffet began investing in Berkshire Hathaway in the early 1960s and soon emerged as a company leader, a position he has kept since then. Today, he serves as both chairman and chief executive, with Omaha-born Charlie Munger a vice chairman.

## The Kiewit Tower

Berkshire Hathaway’s corporate offices in Omaha are located in the Kiewit Tower on 3555 Farnam Street, at the corner of S 36th Street. The building is named after Peter Kiewit Sons’ (The Keiwit Corporation), a construction company which is also headquartered in the building.

## Background

### Berkshire Fine Spinning AssociatesHathaway

* The Berkshire Cotton Manufacturing Company was established in Adams, Massachusetts in 1889. It’s first mill was the Berkshire Mill No. 1, built on Hoosac Street in 1895 by the locally prominent Plunkett family.
* In 1839, Oliver Chace from Massachusetts founded a textile manufacturing company in Valley Falls, Rhode Island, and called it the Valley Falls Company. At this point, Chace already had plenty of experience within the field, having founded his first textile mill back in 1806.

In 1929, the Valley Falls Company merged with the Berkshire Cotton Manufacturing Company, creating the Berkshire Fine Spinning Associates.

### The Hathaway Manufacturing Company

The Hathaway Manufacturing Company was founded by Horatio Hathaway in New Bedford, Massachusetts in 1888. The start up capital for the company was money that Horatio Hathaway had earned from whaling and the China Trade.

### Berkshire Hathaway

Berkshire Hathway was formed in 1955, when Berkshire Fine Spinning Associates merged with the Hathaway Manufacturing Company.

After the merger, Berkshire Hathaway had 15 plants and over 12,000 plant workers. Before the end of the 1950s, seven of the plants had been closed and the workers laid off.

In the early 1960s, investor Warren Buffett noticed that the stock price for Berkshire Hathaway behaved in a predictable manner after each closing of a mill, and in 1962 he began buying stock in the company. Eventually, he realized that the U.S. textile business was in a decline, and when the company president Seabury Stanton made him an oral tender offer of $11 1⁄2 per share for the company to buy back the shares, Buffett accepted. Things turned sour a few weeks later when Buffet received the tender offer in writing, because now the price had been lowered to $11 3⁄8. This angered Buffett, who refused to sell at the lower price and instead started buying up more stock in the company, with the intention of gaining enough control to fire Stanton. Buffett eventually achieved this goal, but at the price of becoming the majority owner of a company in decline.

In 1967, Buffett decided to expand the company into the insurance industry and other investments, to make it less reliant on revenue from the struggling U.S. textile industry. The company’s first foray into the insurance field was the purchase of National Indemnity Company, an insurance company founded in Omaha in 1940 by Jack Debney Ringwalt. Today, it is Berkshire Hathaway’s oldest operating subsidiary.

In 1985, Berkshire Hathaway’s last textile operations were shut down.

In 2010, Buffett said that purchasing Berkshire Hathaway was the largest investment mistake he ever made. He bought a controlling share in the company to get back at Stanton, and it would have been more profitable to invest the money directly in the insurance industry instead.

The company has completed 74 M&A transactions (71 buys, 3 sells), with total acquisition volume of approximately $259.7B. Key M&A activity peaked in 2021 and prior (68 deals), with one deal each in 2022, 2024, and 2026. Top M&A advisors include Wells Fargo Securities, Lazard, and J.P. Morgan Securities (financial), and Munger Tolles & Olson (legal, 10 deals).

**Axa S.A.** is a French [multinational](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_corporation "Multinational corporation") [insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurance "Insurance") corporation headquartered in the [8th arrondissement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_arrondissement_of_Paris "8th arrondissement of Paris") of [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"). It also provides [investment management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Investment_management "Investment management") and other [financial services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_services "Financial services") via its subsidiaries. As of 2024, it is the fourth largest [financial services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Financial_services "Financial services") company by revenue in France, and the eighth [largest French company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_largest_French_companies "List of largest French companies").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The Axa Group operates primarily in [Western Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Europe "Western Europe"), North America, South America, the Indian Pacific region, and the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East "Middle East"), with a presence in Africa as well. It is a component of the [Euro Stoxx 50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro_Stoxx_50 "Euro Stoxx 50") [stock market index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stock_market_index "Stock market index").[[5]](#cite_note-5) In 2023, the company was ranked 48th in the [Forbes Global 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbes_Global_2000 "Forbes Global 2000").[[6]](#cite_note-6)

## Name

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Name")]

Despite being written by the company in upper case, "AXA" is not an [acronym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acronym "Acronym"). It was chosen because its name can be pronounced easily by people who speak any language. After acquiring the Drouot Group in 1982, chairman and CEO [Claude Bébéar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Bébéar "Claude Bébéar") hired an outside consultant to conduct a computer-aided search for a new name. Bébéar wanted a short and snappy name to convey vitality and could be pronounced the same way in every language, consistent with the group's desire for an international presence. Initially, "Elan" was the top choice, but Canadian executives balked because "élan" is the French word for a moose or elk. In 1985, Bébéar chose the name Axa.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

The company was founded in 1816 as Mutuelle del Assurance contre l'Incendie (the Ancienne Mutuelle).[[8]](#cite_note-8) It acquired Compagnie Parisienne de Garantie in 1978 and became Mutuelles Unies.[[9]](#cite_note-history-9) In 1982, it merged with the Drouot Group, owned by the [Hottinguer family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hottinguer_family "Hottinguer family"), becoming Mutuelles Unies/Drouot.

The firm adopted the Axa name in 1986.[[9]](#cite_note-history-9) Axa took over [The Equitable](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Equitable "The Equitable") in 1991[[9]](#cite_note-history-9) and bought Union des Assurances de Paris (UAP), France's largest insurer, in 1996 to become Axa-UAP. It reverted to the name Axa in 1999.[[10]](#cite_note-10) In February 1999, Axa acquired [Guardian Royal Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardian_Royal_Exchange_Assurance "Guardian Royal Exchange Assurance").[[11]](#cite_note-11) In May 2000, it acquired all shares it did not already own in [Sun Life & Provincial Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Life_&_Provincial_Holdings "Sun Life & Provincial Holdings").[[12]](#cite_note-12) On 14 June 2006, Axa acquired [Winterthur Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winterthur_Group "Winterthur Group") from [Credit Suisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Credit_Suisse "Credit Suisse") for approximately €9 billion.[[13]](#cite_note-13) As of 2011, Axa was the second most powerful [transnational corporation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transnational_corporation "Transnational corporation") in terms of [corporate control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporate_power "Corporate power") over [global financial stability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_financial_system "Global financial system").[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15)

In May 2016, the firm announced that it would stop investing in tobacco shares and bonds and allow its portfolio of tobacco-related bonds to run off.[[16]](#cite_note-16) On 12 September 2018, Axa acquired XL Group Ltd., a Bermuda-based property and casualty commercial lines insurer and reinsurer, for $15.3 billion.[[17]](#cite_note-17) In October 2019, the company sold Axa Bank Belgium to [Crelan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crelan "Crelan") for €620 million (US$688.51 million).[[18]](#cite_note-18)[[19]](#cite_note-19)

In 2019, Axa partially disinvested from the Israeli arms group [Elbit Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elbit_Systems "Elbit Systems") following pressure from the [Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boycott,_Divestment_and_Sanctions "Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions") movement.[[20]](#cite_note-FIFAD-20) The move followed several years of campaigning by NGOs, including an April 2018 petition launched by [SumOfUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SumOfUs "SumOfUs") that received 140,000 signatures, leading Axa to "quietly reduce" its investments in Elbit and Israeli banks.[[20]](#cite_note-FIFAD-20) Axa remains indirectly invested in Elbit and Israeli banks through a non-controlling interest in its former subsidiary [Alliance Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alliance_Bernstein "Alliance Bernstein").[[20]](#cite_note-FIFAD-20)

In 2023, Axa has increased investments in Israel as a shareholder in three Israeli banks known to support the [Israeli occupation of the West Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_occupation_of_the_West_Bank "Israeli occupation of the West Bank"): [Bank Hapoalim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Hapoalim "Bank Hapoalim") (US$9.99M), [Bank Leumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_Leumi "Bank Leumi") (US$6M), and [Israel Discount Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel_Discount_Bank "Israel Discount Bank") (US$3.4M). By August 2024, however, AXA had completed a "full divestment" from all three banks, according an analysis by ethical-investing advocacy group [Ekō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekō "Ekō").[[21]](#cite_note-21)

In February 2023, the company sold a 7.94% stake in [Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banca_Monte_dei_Paschi_di_Siena "Banca Monte dei Paschi di Siena") (MPS) to [institutional investors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institutional_investor "Institutional investor"). The package included approximately 100,000,000 MPS [shares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Share_(finance) "Share (finance)") at a price of €2.33 (US$2.50) per share, for a total transaction value of €233 million (US$250 million). Axa retained 0.0007% of the Italian bank's capital.[[22]](#cite_note-22)

Axa Investment Managers acquired France's [Bry-sur-Marne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bry-sur-Marne "Bry-sur-Marne") [film studio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Film_studio "Film studio") and the 12-hectare (30-acre) plot of land on which it is located for €150m in June 2023.[[23]](#cite_note-23)

## Headquarters

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Headquarters")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/48/Palazzo_AXA.JPG/250px-Palazzo_AXA.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Palazzo_AXA.JPG)

Italian Headquarters in [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan")

Axa headquarters is located in the [8th arrondissement of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/8th_arrondissement_of_Paris "8th arrondissement of Paris").[[24]](#cite_note-24) Axa, which already owned 23 Avenue Matignon, acquired the former Hôtel de La Vaupalière, an 18th-century building, in the late 1990s. Architect [Ricardo Bofill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Bofill "Ricardo Bofill") integrated the facade of the hotel with a modern glass building that covers the courtyard that the hotel also occupies. The complex serves as Axa's head office.[[25]](#cite_note-25)

## Operations

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Operations")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/AXA_Group_Global_Locations.svg/500px-AXA_Group_Global_Locations.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AXA_Group_Global_Locations.svg)

Axa Group global locations

### United Kingdom

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: United Kingdom")]

Axa trades in the United Kingdom as Axa UK, with subsidiaries including Axa Insurance, Axa Wealth and Axa Health. Axa PPP International was the trading name for Axa PPP healthcare's international health insurance division, which was later rebranded as Axa Global Healthcare on 1 January 2017. The company bought the online insurer [Swiftcover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiftcover "Swiftcover"), which was notorious for its controversial [Iggy Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iggy_Pop "Iggy Pop") TV advertising campaign, which was subsequently banned for being misleading, on the grounds that Iggy Pop would not be eligible for cover as someone working in the entertainment industry.[[27]](#cite_note-27)

In September 2013, Axa Wealth was fined £1.8 million by the FCA for failing to ensure it gave suitable investment advice to its customers. The regulator says it found "serious defects" in the way Axa advisers in Clydesdale Bank, Yorkshire Bank and the West Bromwich Building Society advised customers on investments.[[28]](#cite_note-28)

In 2018, they became the 'Official Global Insurance' partner of [Premier League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_League "Premier League") team [Liverpool F.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") and in 2019, began sponsoring the training kits of the team.[[29]](#cite_note-29) In 2020, the partnership was cemented further, when they purchased the naming rights to the club's [newly built training centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Academy,_Kirkby "The Academy, Kirkby"), which became officially known as 'The AXA Training Centre.'[[30]](#cite_note-30)

In 2016, Axa Wealth was sold to the Phoenix Group, which later changed its name to [Standard Life plc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standard_Life_plc "Standard Life plc") in 2026.[[31]](#cite_note-31)

### Axa Health

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Axa Health")]

Axa Health sells [private medical insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_medical_insurance "Private medical insurance") in the UK and was known as Axa PPP Healthcare until 2020.[[32]](#cite_note-32) It was previously the London Association for Hospital Services, set up in 1938 as a private healthcare scheme for people of middle income in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London").[[33]](#cite_note-33)[[34]](#cite_note-34) It was incorporated in 1940 with assistance from the [British Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Medical_Association "British Medical Association"), the [King's Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King's_Fund "King's Fund"), and the [medical royal colleges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_royal_colleges "Medical royal colleges").[[35]](#cite_note-35)

[Guardian Royal Exchange Assurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardian_Royal_Exchange_Assurance "Guardian Royal Exchange Assurance") bought it in 1998 for £435 million; a year later it was bought by [Sun Life & Provincial Holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axa_Sun_Life "Axa Sun Life"), an Axa subsidiary.[[36]](#cite_note-36)

### Axa Global Healthcare

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Axa Global Healthcare")]

Axa Global Healthcare has previously been known as Axa PPP International, Axa Global Protect or Axa Healthcare Management. In 2017, the [subsidiary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subsidiary "Subsidiary") Axa Global Healthcare became an independent Managing General Agent, selling and administering international health insurance products. While Axa Health provides insurance across the UK, Axa - Global Healthcare caters to those needing [health insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_insurance "Health insurance") around the world.[[37]](#cite_note-AXA_Global_Healthcare_Journey_-_About_Us-37)

In 2018, Axa Global Healthcare launched a Virtual Doctor service for its customers with outpatient cover and in 2020 offered it across all plans.[[38]](#cite_note-AXA_–_Global_Healthcare_introduces_virtual_doctor_service-38) Provided by [Teladoc Health](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teladoc_Health "Teladoc Health"), it offers anytime access to medical advice by phone or video by doctors located around the world who speak more than 15 languages and is targeted at [expatriates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expatriates "Expatriates").[[39]](#cite_note-39)

### Axa Ireland

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Axa Ireland")]

Axa established a presence in Ireland in 1999 when it bought British-based [Guardian Royal Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guardian_Royal_Exchange "Guardian Royal Exchange"),[[40]](#cite_note-40) which had previously acquired PMPA.[[41]](#cite_note-irishtimes.com-41) PMPA, Private Motorists Protection Association,[[42]](#cite_note-42) was at the time one of Ireland's biggest insurance companies. It is the third-largest general insurer in the Republic of Ireland.[[41]](#cite_note-irishtimes.com-41)

In August 2023, it was announced Axa had acquired the [Little Island, Cork](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Island,_Cork "Little Island, Cork")-headquartered health insurance company, [Laya Healthcare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laya_Healthcare "Laya Healthcare") for €650 million.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

### Axa Canada

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Axa Canada")]

Axa Canada marketed insurance in [Quebec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quebec "Quebec"), [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario"), [Western Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Canada "Western Canada") and [Atlantic Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Canada "Atlantic Canada"). In 2009 it had a total of approximately 2300 employees and 4000 brokers and advisors. The head office was in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), Quebec. In 2011 it was sold to [Intact Financial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intact_Financial "Intact Financial") Corp. for C$2.6 billion.[[44]](#cite_note-44)

### AXA United States

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: AXA United States")]

The American arm of Axa is *Axa Financial, Inc.*, which is known mainly through its subsidiaries such as *Axa Advisors*, *Axa Network*, *[MONY](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MONY "MONY")* (formerly [Mutual of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_of_New_York "Mutual of New York")), *US Financial Life*, and *[AllianceBernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AllianceBernstein "AllianceBernstein")*.[[45]](#cite_note-45) The Equitable was acquired in 1991; the [Mutual Life Insurance Company of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_Life_Insurance_Company_of_New_York "Mutual Life Insurance Company of New York") (MONY) was acquired in 2004.[[46]](#cite_note-46)[[47]](#cite_note-47)

Axa's US operations are incorporated in Delaware.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

### Mexico

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Mexico")]

In July 2008, Axa acquired ING Insurance Mexico, offering essentially the same services that ING offered. Axa then sued an [ING Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ING_Group "ING Group") subsidiary over alleged misrepresentations in the $1.5 billion sale stating it suffered "tens (if not hundreds) of millions of dollars in damages."[[49]](#cite_note-AXA_sues_ING-49)

### Australia

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Australia")]

In 1995 the Axa Group purchased a 51 per cent controlling interest in Australian life insurer, [National Mutual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Mutual "National Mutual")[[50]](#cite_note-50)[[51]](#cite_note-51) It was rebranded Axa.[[52]](#cite_note-52)[[53]](#cite_note-53) In March 2011, Axa agreed to merge its Australian operations with [AMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AMP_Limited "AMP Limited") under the AMP brand.[[54]](#cite_note-54)[[55]](#cite_note-55)[[56]](#cite_note-56)

### Africa

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Africa")]

In April 2016 Axa unveiled a partnership with Lloyd's of London insurer Chaucer Holdings to enter the growing market of speciality insurance in Africa. Axa Africa Specialty Risks helps to mitigate risks through its coverholder, Chaucer Syndicate 1084 and Axa Africa Specialty Risks 6130. Axa ASR focuses on specialty and corporate lines, with coverage and an on-the-ground presence across Africa. Axa and Lloyd's both have excellent international financial strength ratings (AA- by Fitch and A+ by Standard & Poor's). The lines of business include: Political Risk, Political Violence and Terrorism, Energy, Construction, Property, Liability, Marine and Aviation. Since 2014 Axa has made several acquisitions of other insurers in an attempt to expand. Axa already operates in Cameroon, Egypt, Gabon, Ivory Coast, Morocco, Nigeria, Senegal and Algeria.[[57]](#cite_note-AXA_SA-57) Axa Africa also has a role in the trade between Asia and some African countries.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

### Kamet Ventures

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Kamet Ventures")]

In January 2016, Axa created Kamet Ventures, an insurtech incubator, to build disruptive businesses in the insurance, healthcare and assistance space with an initial funding of €100 million. Some of Kamet's investments include an insurance advice platform, [Anorak Technologies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anorak_Technologies?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anorak Technologies (page does not exist)") and an elderly care platform, Birdie.[[59]](#cite_note-59)[[60]](#cite_note-60)[[61]](#cite_note-61)

### Axa Investment Managers

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Axa Investment Managers")]

Main article: [Axa Investment Managers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axa_Investment_Managers "Axa Investment Managers")

Axa Investment Managers (Axa IM), was a global investment management company with offices in over 22 locations worldwide. As of 31 December 2020, it managed over €858 billion in assets on behalf of institutional and retail clients. It operated as the investment arm for Axa. In December 2024 it was acquired by BNP Paribas.

### Axa Hong Kong & Macau

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Axa Hong Kong & Macau")]

Axa Asia Pacific Holdings Limited acquired MLC (Hong Kong) Limited and re-branded it as Axa (Hong Kong) Life Insurance Company Limited in 2006.[[62]](#cite_note-62)

### Former holdings

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Axa&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Former holdings")]

Further information: [SunLife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SunLife "SunLife")

In 2010, Axa sold a UK business unit called [SunLife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SunLife "SunLife") to [Resolution Limited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resolution_Limited "Resolution Limited").[[63]](#cite_note-63)

In 2021, the [Gulf Insurance Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_Insurance_Group?action=edit&redlink=1 "Gulf Insurance Group (page does not exist)") acquired Axa's holdings in the Gulf region, rebranding them as GIG in the Middle East.[[64]](#cite_note-64)

args.summary:
Axa S.A. is a French multinational insurance corporation headquartered in Paris, founded in 1816 (as Mutuelle del Assurance contre l'Incendie) and adopting the Axa name in 1986. It is the fourth largest financial services company by revenue in France and the eighth largest French company, operating in Western Europe, North America, South America, the Indian Pacific region, the Middle East, and Africa. As of 2024, Axa reported revenue of €87.3 billion, net income of €8.07 billion, total assets of €653.76 billion, and approximately 113,696 employees. The company is publicly traded on Euronext Paris and is a component of the CAC 40 and Euro Stoxx 50 indices.

Key historical milestones include: acquiring The Equitable (1991), buying Union des Assurances de Paris (UAP) in 1996, acquiring Guardian Royal Exchange (1999), Sun Life & Provincial Holdings (2000), Winterthur Group from Credit Suisse for €9 billion (2006), and XL Group Ltd. for $15.3 billion (2018). In 2024, Axa Investment Managers was acquired by BNP Paribas.

The company provides insurance (general, health, vehicle, travel, home, life, pet), mortgage loans, investment management, asset management, and mutual funds. Its subsidiaries include Axa Bank Belgium (sold to Crelan in 2019), Axa Investment Managers, and Axa XL. Axa's operations span the UK, Ireland, Canada (sold 2011), the US, Mexico, Australia (merged with AMP in 2011), Africa, Hong Kong & Macau, through Kamet Ventures (an insurtech incubator), and others.

Axa has faced controversies including fines for investment advice failures, lawsuits over acquisitions, and pressure from the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement regarding investments in Israeli arms and banks. In 2016, Axa stopped investing in tobacco. In 2024, it completed a full divestment from three Israeli banks (Bank Hapoalim, Bank Leumi, Israel Discount Bank).

# AXA Strategy and Business Model

## Executive Overview

AXA, legally AXA SA, is one of the world’s largest multiline insurers, with operations spanning retail property and casualty insurance, commercial and specialty insurance, health, life and protection, savings, and related assistance services. Its roots date to 1816 through French mutual insurers, and the modern group was assembled over decades through acquisitions and portfolio reshaping before adopting the AXA name in 1985. Headquartered in Paris, AXA has a particularly strong base in Europe and a global commercial-lines platform through AXA XL.

The strategy of AXA today is not to be every kind of financial-services company. Management’s 2024-2026 plan emphasizes higher-quality insurance earnings: growing property and casualty, health, and protection businesses; improving technical excellence in underwriting and claims; simplifying the portfolio; and deploying capital selectively. That focus matters because the economics of insurance depend less on headline volume than on pricing discipline, claims performance, capital strength, and cash remittances from regulated local entities. AXA serves households, small businesses, employers, and large multinational corporations through agents, brokers, banks, partners, and digital channels. In FY2024, AXA reported gross written premiums and other revenues of €110.3 billion.

## AXA at a Glance

| Logo |
| --- |
| Common name | AXA |
| Full legal name | AXA SA |
| Headquarters | Paris, France |
| Ownership | Public company; listed in Paris. Mutuelles AXA is the principal long-term shareholder and held a significant minority stake as of FY2024. |
| Ticker | CS |
| Exchange | EPA - Euronext Paris |
| Market Cap | $116.12B |
| Revenue (FY2024) | €110.30B |
| Founding / major historical milestones | Roots trace to 1816 in France; AXA name adopted in 1985; merger with UAP in 1996; acquisition of Winterthur in 2006; acquisition of XL Group in 2018. |
| Industry or industries | Insurance; commercial and specialty risk; health and employee benefits; assistance services |
| Key products or services | Motor and home insurance, health insurance, life and protection, savings and retirement products, employee benefits, commercial property and casualty insurance, specialty insurance, reinsurance, and assistance services |
| Geographic footprint | Global, with core positions in France and Europe, selected operations in Asia, Africa, Latin America, and a worldwide commercial-risk platform through AXA XL |
| Business segments as officially reported | France; Europe; AXA XL; Asia, Africa & EME-LATAM; Transversal & Central Holdings (FY2024 reporting structure) |
| Company website | <https://www.axa.com/> |

## 1. What Is the Strategy of AXA?

1. ### 1a. What is the winning aspiration of AXA?

   AXA’s stated purpose is to *act for human progress by protecting what matters*. In strategic terms, “winning” appears to mean being a leading global insurer in protection-oriented lines while producing resilient earnings, strong cash remittance, and durable capital strength. AXA’s 2024-2026 “Unlock the Future” plan translated that aspiration into measurable financial goals, including annual growth in underlying earnings per share of 6% to 8% and cumulative organic cash remittance of more than €21 billion over the period. Just as important, AXA has signaled that it does not define success as maximum scale in every financial product. It increasingly defines success as profitable growth in lines where underwriting skill, claims execution, distribution reach, and capital discipline create defensible economics.
2. ### 1b. Where does AXA play?

   AXA plays in multiline insurance, with the clearest emphasis on property and casualty insurance, commercial and specialty risk, health, employee benefits, and protection. It also remains active in life, savings, and retirement products, but its strategic center of gravity has shifted toward protection-heavy businesses rather than purely savings-led ones. Geographically, AXA plays from a strong European base, with France as a home market, broad positions across continental Europe, selected operations in Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East, and a global commercial footprint through AXA XL. Its customer scope ranges from retail households and small businesses to mid-market companies, multinationals, and institutional buyers of employee-benefits solutions.
3. ### 1c. How does AXA plan to win?

   AXA’s plan to win rests on a combination of technical excellence and scale. In practice, that means pricing risk accurately, keeping underwriting discipline even when markets soften, managing claims effectively, and using a broad distribution footprint to retain and deepen customer relationships. In retail insurance, AXA seeks to win through trust, brand, product breadth, and service quality. In commercial lines, especially through AXA XL, it competes more on specialist expertise, broker relationships, risk engineering, and portfolio steering. Across the group, AXA is also trying to improve its business mix by emphasizing property and casualty, health, and protection businesses that appear to offer better earnings quality than some more capital-intensive or market-sensitive savings activities.
4. ### 1d. What capabilities must AXA have in place?

   To execute that strategy, AXA needs strong actuarial and underwriting capabilities, advanced claims management, disciplined reserving, reinsurance expertise, and sophisticated investment and asset-liability management. It also needs country-level regulatory capability because insurance is regulated locally, not globally. On the commercial side, AXA must sustain deep broker and partner relationships, especially in large corporate risk. On the operating side, data, digital platforms, analytics, fraud detection, and customer-service tools are increasingly necessary to control expense ratios and improve retention. In health and employee benefits, the company also needs network management, service administration, and prevention-oriented capabilities, not just insurance manufacturing.
5. ### 1e. What management systems does AXA require?

   AXA requires management systems that balance growth with prudence. For an insurer, that means capital and solvency management under Solvency II, risk committees, underwriting authorities, catastrophe and exposure controls, reserving governance, and regular portfolio reviews. It also means tracking operational measures such as combined ratio, pricing adequacy, claims severity and frequency, policy retention, productivity, and cash remittance from subsidiaries to the holding company. Because AXA is highly decentralized legally but must still act like one group strategically, it also needs strong country governance, central standards for risk and technology, and clear capital-allocation rules. Those systems are critical to ensuring that local growth does not come at the expense of group profitability or balance-sheet resilience.

## 2. What Are the Current Strategic Initiatives of AXA?

AXA’s current strategic initiatives are best understood through its 2024-2026 plan and related disclosures. The themes are consistent: improve the business mix, sharpen technical execution, simplify the portfolio, and use technology to raise productivity and service quality.

* **Grow higher-quality protection businesses.** AXA has been leaning into property and casualty, health, and protection lines rather than pursuing volume equally across all product categories. This reflects management’s view that these businesses offer better earnings quality and more attractive long-term economics than some lower-margin or more capital-market-sensitive savings activities.
* **Strengthen technical performance in retail and commercial P&C.** In both retail P&C and AXA XL, AXA has emphasized pricing adequacy, portfolio steering, claims discipline, and better selection of risk. This is especially important after several years in which inflation, catastrophe losses, and specialty-market volatility tested the industry’s underwriting discipline.
* **Scale health and employee benefits.** AXA has identified health as a structural growth area, supported by aging populations, employer demand for benefits, and pressure on public health systems in many markets. The opportunity is not just to sell insurance policies, but also to improve service, prevention, and customer experience.
* **Simplify the group and focus capital on core insurance.** AXA has been reshaping the portfolio to sharpen its identity as a global insurer. The agreed sale of AXA Investment Managers, disclosed in 2024, fit that logic by emphasizing insurance and capital discipline over maintaining a broader asset-management footprint.
* **Use data, digital tools, and AI to improve service and efficiency.** AXA has publicly discussed technology and AI as practical enablers in underwriting, claims, customer service, fraud detection, and employee productivity. The strategic aim is not technology for its own sake, but faster cycle times, better risk selection, and lower cost to serve.
* **Maintain strong solvency and cash generation.** AXA continues to frame capital strength and cash remittance as strategic assets. That gives the group flexibility to invest in growth, absorb volatility, and return capital to shareholders without compromising resilience.

## 3. What Is the Business Model of AXA?

AXA’s business model is fundamentally an insurance model, not a conventional product-manufacturing model. Customers pay premiums for protection, savings wrappers, benefits administration, or risk-transfer capacity. AXA then earns returns by underwriting risk better than it prices it, controlling expenses, managing claims well, and investing the premium float and capital base prudently.

* **What customers actually buy:** Retail customers buy protection for cars, homes, health, income, life, and savings goals. Employers buy employee-benefits coverage and related services. Corporate clients buy risk transfer for property, casualty, cyber, marine, aviation, professional, and other specialty exposures.
* **Recurring or repeat-driven versus one-time:** Much of AXA’s model is recurring. Motor, home, health, and commercial policies typically renew annually. Group benefits and corporate programs can be sticky if service and pricing remain competitive. Some life and savings flows are more episodic, but the installed base creates recurring fees, spread income, and renewal opportunities.
* **How pricing power works:** AXA’s pricing power comes from actuarial insight, brand trust, distribution access, and its willingness to reprice or reshape portfolios when loss trends worsen. In insurance, pricing power is rarely unconstrained. It is bounded by regulation, competition, broker influence, and customers’ ability to switch at renewal.
* **Why the business mix matters:** AXA has clearly been steering toward protection-heavy lines. Property and casualty, health, and commercial specialty businesses tend to have more visible technical economics than savings-led activities, which can be more sensitive to financial markets, guarantees, and interest-rate conditions.
* **What drives margins and cash generation:** For AXA, “gross margin” is not the most useful lens. More relevant drivers are combined ratio, claims frequency and severity, reserve development, expense ratio, investment income, product mix, and capital intensity. Cash generation depends heavily on dividends and remittances from regulated operating entities, not just accounting profit.
* **Revenue model:** The model is primarily premium-based, supplemented by fee income on some savings and services activities and by investment income on the asset base backing liabilities and shareholder funds.

## 4. What Products and Services Does AXA Sell?

AXA sells a broad range of insurance and related services, but the most strategically important offerings are now concentrated in protection-led categories.

* **Retail property and casualty insurance:** Motor, home, personal liability, travel, and other personal-lines products sold to households and small businesses.
* **Commercial property and casualty insurance:** Coverage for businesses ranging from mid-market companies to large multinationals, including property, casualty, workers’ compensation in relevant markets, professional lines, and specialty risks.
* **Specialty insurance and reinsurance through AXA XL:** AXA XL extends the group into global specialty markets such as cyber, marine, aviation, construction, political risk, and certain reinsurance lines. This is strategically important because it differentiates AXA from purely domestic or retail-led insurers.
* **Health and employee benefits:** Individual and group health coverage, supplemental health, employee-benefits solutions, and related service capabilities. Health is one of AXA’s main growth priorities.
* **Life, protection, savings, and retirement:** Life insurance, income protection, credit protection, unit-linked savings, retirement, and other long-term financial-protection products. These remain important, but AXA’s strategic emphasis has been more on protection than on purely savings accumulation.
* **Assistance and partner-distributed services:** Travel assistance, mobility and roadside assistance, and other services distributed through partners in selected markets.

From a strategic standpoint, AXA’s retail and commercial P&C businesses, health, and protection products appear to carry the greatest current importance. Savings and retirement products remain meaningful, but they are less central to the group’s recent strategic narrative than they were in earlier periods.

## 5. What Are the Key Competitors or Peers of AXA?

Competition varies by geography and business line. No single rival overlaps perfectly with AXA across every market, but the following companies are among the closest competitors or peers.

| Company | Relationship to AXA | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Allianz | Direct global multiline peer | Large European insurer with strong positions in P&C, life, asset management, and commercial insurance. |
| Zurich Insurance Group | Direct global multiline peer | Competes in retail and commercial insurance, especially in corporate and international programs. |
| Generali | European multiline competitor | Major rival in life and P&C across continental Europe, with overlap in several AXA markets. |
| Chubb | Commercial and specialty competitor | Strong benchmark in underwriting discipline and a close peer to AXA XL in commercial and specialty lines. |
| AIG | Commercial and specialty competitor | Competes with AXA XL in large corporate, specialty, and multinational insurance programs. |
| Crédit Agricole Assurances | Regional and bancassurance competitor | Important French competitor through bank-led distribution in savings, protection, and P&C. |
| BNP Paribas Cardif | Regional and bancassurance competitor | Competes in savings, protection, creditor insurance, and partner-distributed insurance, especially in France and selected international markets. |
| MetLife | Life and employee-benefits peer | Relevant comparator in group benefits, protection, and corporate employee-benefits solutions. |
| Prudential plc | Asia-focused peer | Useful comparison point for AXA’s Asian life and health operations and growth-market strategy. |
| Munich Re / ERGO | Partial peer | Overlap exists in reinsurance, specialty risk, and certain retail markets, though not across AXA’s full scope. |

## 6. What Is the Marketing Strategy of AXA?

AXA’s marketing strategy reflects the reality that insurance is a trust purchase. In retail markets, brand matters because customers are buying a promise that may not be tested until a claim occurs. AXA therefore uses brand marketing to reinforce reliability, protection, and reassurance, while local businesses support that with product campaigns, digital acquisition, retention marketing, and partner-led distribution programs. Marketing is especially relevant in personal lines, health, and direct channels, where awareness and conversion matter.

In commercial and specialty insurance, marketing looks different. The key levers are broker relationships, specialist reputation, risk-engineering credibility, thought leadership, and tailored propositions for industries or complex exposures. That means AXA XL relies less on mass marketing and more on expert-led go-to-market activity. Overall, marketing appears to be an important supporting capability for AXA, but not the main source of competitive advantage on its own. Distribution strength, technical pricing, and claims execution are at least as important as brand advertising.

## 7. What Are the Key Customer Segments of AXA?

AXA serves a broad set of customer groups, which is one reason its earnings base is relatively diversified.

* **Retail households:** Individuals and families buying motor, home, health, life, protection, savings, and retirement products.
* **Small and medium-sized businesses:** Smaller commercial clients buying property, casualty, liability, fleet, and employee-related cover.
* **Mid-market and large corporates:** Businesses that need broader commercial insurance programs, including multinational coordination and specialist cover.
* **Large global and specialty-risk clients:** Multinational corporations using AXA XL for complex property, casualty, specialty, and reinsurance-related solutions.
* **Employers and institutions:** Buyers of employee benefits, group health, and related services.
* **Savers and retirement customers:** Customers using life and savings products as long-term financial-protection and wealth-accumulation vehicles.
* **Distribution partners:** Banks, affinity partners, and other intermediaries that help AXA reach end customers in certain markets.

AXA is diversified, but its center of gravity remains European retail and protection markets plus global commercial insurance through AXA XL.

## 8. What Is the Sales Model of AXA?

AXA uses a multi-channel sales model because insurance distribution is highly local and product-specific. It sells through proprietary agents and advisors in some markets, through independent brokers in others, through bank partnerships and affinity channels, and through digital direct channels where customer acquisition economics are attractive. That gives AXA reach, but it also means channel management is a core operating discipline.

* **Retail and mass-market insurance:** Often sold through agents, bank partners, contact centers, websites, and apps.
* **Commercial insurance:** Frequently distributed through brokers, especially for mid-market and large-corporate accounts.
* **Global corporate and specialty insurance:** Typically sold through expert teams working with major brokers and risk managers.
* **Employee benefits and health:** Sold through employer-facing teams, consultants, brokers, and corporate relationships.
* **Partner channels:** AXA also reaches customers through embedded, white-label, or affinity-style partnerships in selected product areas.

This channel structure affects growth and profitability. Broad distribution reduces dependence on any one route to market, but it increases complexity and can create channel conflict. It also affects pricing power: brokered commercial business tends to be more transparently priced, while proprietary retail channels can support stronger cross-sell and retention if service quality is high.

## 9. In What Geographies Does AXA Operate?

AXA operates globally, but its footprint is not uniform. Europe remains the core of the group, and France is the home market. Beyond that, AXA has a meaningful presence in several other European countries, selected higher-growth markets in Asia, Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East, and a broad global commercial-risk network through AXA XL.

* **France:** Core retail, health, life, and commercial market, and the location of group headquarters.
* **Europe:** Major operations across countries including Germany, Switzerland, Belgium, Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom, Ireland, and Luxembourg.
* **AXA XL global platform:** Commercial and specialty insurance presence spanning North America, the London market, Bermuda, continental Europe, and Asia-Pacific hubs.
* **Asia, Africa, and Latin America:** Selected country positions rather than blanket coverage, giving AXA exposure to growth markets without attempting to be dominant everywhere.

Insurance is regulated locally, so AXA’s geographic model is built around local legal entities and licenses rather than a single global operating company. One useful way to think about AXA is that it is a federation of local insurers, tied together by capital, brand, technology, and risk standards. AXA XL adds a more globally integrated layer on top of that local model.

## 10. Who Are the Owners of AXA?

AXA SA is a publicly traded company listed in Paris. As disclosed in FY2024 materials, Mutuelles AXA is the company’s principal long-term shareholder and holds a significant minority stake. The remainder of the share register is widely held among institutional investors, retail investors, and employees. AXA is not majority-owned by a government or private-equity sponsor.

## 11. How Is AXA Organized?

Legally, AXA SA is the listed parent company. Beneath it sits a large network of locally regulated insurance subsidiaries, branches, service companies, and holding entities. That legal structure is necessary because insurance licenses, reserving rules, capital requirements, and consumer regulations are country-specific.

Managerially, AXA is organized by a mix of geography and business line. In FY2024 reporting, the main segments were France, Europe, AXA XL, Asia, Africa & EME-LATAM, and Transversal & Central Holdings. AXA XL is particularly important because it is not just another country unit; it is the group’s global commercial and specialty platform.

At a practical level, AXA operates with local country leadership for domestic markets, global leadership for AXA XL and other transversal activities, and central group functions for finance, risk, strategy, technology, human resources, investments, and governance. This makes AXA neither fully centralized nor fully decentralized. The group sets standards and allocates capital centrally, but execution happens largely through country businesses and specialized global units.

## 12. How Does AXA Operate?

AXA’s day-to-day operation revolves around managing risk promises at scale. The business looks different from a manufacturer or retailer because the core tasks are underwriting, service, claims settlement, capital management, and investing assets against future liabilities.

1. **Product design and pricing:** AXA designs policies for specific customer segments, prices them using actuarial models, and updates terms as claims trends, inflation, and regulation evolve.
2. **Distribution and new business acquisition:** Country units, agents, brokers, banks, and digital channels originate business. In commercial lines, underwriters and client teams work closely with brokers and risk managers.
3. **Underwriting and risk selection:** AXA decides which risks to accept, on what terms, with what limits, and at what price. This is especially important in commercial and specialty lines, where a few badly underwritten accounts can materially affect profitability.
4. **Policy administration and servicing:** The company collects premiums, handles endorsements and renewals, and services customers through contact centers, digital channels, intermediaries, and operations teams.
5. **Claims management:** Claims handling is one of AXA’s most important operational activities. Speed, leakage control, fraud detection, litigation management, and customer communication all affect both customer satisfaction and combined ratio.
6. **Reinsurance and exposure management:** AXA cedes part of its risk to reinsurers, manages catastrophe exposures, and monitors accumulations across geographies and lines of business.
7. **Investment and capital management:** Premiums and reserves are invested subject to liability matching, solvency constraints, and risk appetite. Local entities then upstream cash to the group when allowed by regulation and capital conditions.

The biggest operational complexities include inflation in claims costs, catastrophe volatility, cyber and specialty-risk accumulation, regulatory variation across countries, and the challenge of modernizing legacy policy and claims systems without disrupting service.

## 13. What Are the Growth Opportunities for AXA?

Management-stated priorities and a reasonable external synthesis point to several credible growth opportunities for AXA.

* **Commercial and specialty insurance:** AXA XL gives the group exposure to large global risk markets where demand for cyber, specialty, and multinational programs remains structurally relevant.
* **Health and employee benefits:** Rising healthcare demand, aging populations, and employer interest in benefits can support growth in both premiums and service-based offerings.
* **Retail P&C repricing and retention:** In markets where AXA has strong local scale, it can grow by passing through claims inflation, improving segmentation, and lifting retention through better service and bundling.
* **Protection-led life business:** Life and protection products tied to mortality, morbidity, and income protection can be more strategically attractive than pure savings accumulation.
* **Productivity from technology and AI:** Faster claims handling, better fraud detection, improved underwriting support, and lower servicing cost can expand earnings even without dramatic top-line acceleration.
* **Selected growth markets:** Asia, Africa, and Latin America remain logical expansion areas where AXA already has footholds and can grow through local scale, partnerships, or targeted investment.
* **Capital redeployment after portfolio simplification:** As AXA reshapes the group around core insurance, it may have more flexibility to reinvest in businesses with better strategic fit and returns.

The main constraints are also clear: catastrophe losses, reserve risk, regulatory change, intense competition in commoditized retail lines, distribution economics, and the fact that insurance growth must remain disciplined. For AXA, poorly priced growth would destroy value faster than slow, well-priced growth.

## 14. What Is the History of AXA?

AXA’s roots go back to 1816 through French mutual insurers, but the modern company was built much later through consolidation and international expansion. Claude Bébéar is the central architect of modern AXA, having helped assemble the group through a series of acquisitions and strategic moves.

* **1816:** Origins in French mutual insurance.
* **1985:** The group adopted the AXA name, chosen in part because it is short and works across languages.
* **1991-1992:** AXA acquired a controlling interest in The Equitable in the United States, a major step in international expansion.
* **1996:** Merger with UAP, one of the defining deals in AXA’s development into a global insurer.
* **1999:** Acquisition of Guardian Royal Exchange, strengthening the company’s position in the United Kingdom and other markets.
* **2006:** Acquisition of Winterthur from Credit Suisse, expanding AXA’s scale in Europe and selected international markets.
* **2018:** Acquisition of XL Group, which materially increased AXA’s exposure to commercial P&C and specialty insurance and led to the AXA XL platform.
* **2018-2020:** Separation from much of the former U.S. life and asset-accumulation exposure through the Equitable Holdings transaction and subsequent exits, reflecting portfolio reshaping.
* **2024:** AXA announced the agreed sale of AXA Investment Managers to BNP Paribas, signaling a further sharpening of focus on core insurance activities.

The long arc of AXA’s history shows a pattern: use large transactions selectively to change the business mix, then spend years integrating and simplifying.

## 15. What Are the Key Brands Owned by AXA?

Brand matters at AXA, especially in consumer insurance and employer-facing health markets. The group’s brand architecture is relatively straightforward compared with many diversified financial institutions.

* **AXA:** The master brand used across much of the group’s retail, health, life, and general-insurance footprint. Its role is to signal trust, scale, and continuity.
* **AXA XL:** The commercial and specialty brand created after the XL Group acquisition. It matters because large corporate and specialty clients value technical reputation and broker familiarity.
* **AXA Health:** Used in health-related offerings in selected markets, supporting AXA’s strategic emphasis on health and employee benefits.
* **AXA Partners:** Associated with assistance, mobility, travel, and partner-distributed services in relevant markets.

Brand is a major strategic lever in retail and health because customer trust affects acquisition and renewal. In wholesale specialty insurance, however, technical credibility and broker relationships can matter more than consumer-style brand advertising.

## 16. How Is AXA Using AI?

AXA has publicly discussed using data science, machine learning, and more recently generative artificial intelligence across a range of operational use cases. The company’s AI posture appears pragmatic: use AI to improve underwriting, claims, service, and productivity rather than position AI as a stand-alone business line.

* **Claims operations:** Automation of document intake, triage, fraud detection, and parts of claims assessment where image analysis or pattern recognition can improve speed and consistency.
* **Underwriting and pricing support:** Better risk segmentation, portfolio monitoring, and decision support for underwriters, especially in data-rich lines.
* **Customer service:** Digital assistants, workflow support, and knowledge retrieval tools that help service teams respond faster and more consistently.
* **Operational productivity:** Summarization, document handling, and employee-copilot use cases that can reduce manual administrative work.

Some of these uses are mature extensions of traditional analytics; generative AI is newer and more controlled. For AXA, the key constraints are governance, data privacy, model risk, explainability, and regulatory compliance, all of which matter more in insurance than in many less regulated sectors.

## 17. What Is the Technology Strategy of AXA?

AXA’s technology strategy appears centered on modernizing core insurance operations rather than turning the group into a software vendor. The priorities are likely to include core-system simplification, better data architecture, digital customer journeys, automation, analytics, and stronger cybersecurity. In a large insurer, technology is central because service speed, claims quality, fraud control, and underwriting precision depend heavily on system quality.

In retail insurance, technology supports online acquisition, policy servicing, claims tracking, and cross-sell. In commercial insurance, it supports underwriting workbenches, exposure management, broker connectivity, and portfolio analytics. Across the group, cloud migration, APIs, data platforms, and cyber resilience are important because AXA operates through many country entities and legacy stacks. Technology is therefore both an internal enabler and, indirectly, part of the customer proposition: better systems usually mean faster service, more accurate pricing, and lower operating cost.

## 18. What Is the Finance Strategy of AXA?

AXA’s finance strategy is to turn diversified insurance earnings into dependable cash remittance while preserving strong capital ratios and balance-sheet flexibility. For an insurer, that means finance is inseparable from risk management. The company has to decide not only how much to grow, but which lines deserve capital, how much risk to retain, what to cede to reinsurers, and how to invest assets backing liabilities.

At a high level, AXA’s finance strategy supports the broader corporate strategy in four ways. First, it favors businesses with stronger earnings quality, which helps explain the emphasis on P&C, health, and protection. Second, it uses solvency and cash-remittance targets as operating disciplines, not just reporting metrics. Third, it supports shareholder distributions through dividends and selective buybacks while still funding technology, distribution, and underwriting capabilities. Fourth, it uses portfolio reshaping to sharpen returns rather than simply accumulate assets.

Management’s 2024-2026 plan included objectives such as 6% to 8% annual growth in underlying earnings per share and more than €21 billion of cumulative organic cash remittance. Those targets are a useful summary of AXA’s finance strategy: profitable growth, disciplined capital allocation, and strong cash conversion from local entities to the parent company.

## 19. What Major Acquisitions Has AXA Made?

Acquisitions have played a major role in AXA’s history, although the group’s recent pattern is selective portfolio reshaping rather than constant dealmaking. The most important transactions changed AXA’s geographic reach or business mix.

| Year | Transaction | Strategic significance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1991-1992 | The Equitable | Expanded AXA into the United States and marked a major step in its internationalization. |
| 1996 | UAP merger | Transformational deal that made AXA one of the largest global insurers. |
| 1999 | Guardian Royal Exchange | Strengthened AXA’s scale in the U.K. and other markets. |
| 2006 | Winterthur | Added scale in Europe and selected international markets and deepened AXA’s multinational profile. |
| 2018 | XL Group | One of AXA’s most strategically important modern acquisitions, shifting the group toward commercial P&C and specialty insurance through AXA XL. |

Recent deal behavior also shows that AXA uses divestitures as a strategic tool. The agreed sale of AXA Investment Managers, announced in 2024, is an example of portfolio simplification rather than expansion. Taken together, AXA’s M&A record suggests that the company uses transactions to change its business mix, not just to add scale.

## 20. How Companies Like AXA Leverage Independent Consultants through Umbrex

Umbrex has built a global community of more than 8,000 independent management consultants based in over 50 countries. These consultants are alumni of McKinsey, Bain, BCG, and other top firms. Companies like AXA use Umbrex when they want that level of strategic and functional capability without commissioning a full consulting team and its associated overhead. Umbrex consultants work across strategy, operations, organization, marketing, sales, finance, technology, ERP, and AI.

For a company like AXA, the most valuable projects are usually focused, high-impact assignments tied to underwriting performance, distribution, claims, technology, growth, or portfolio change. Representative examples include:

* Commercial-lines portfolio profitability diagnostics for AXA XL by line, broker, country, and client segment.
* Retail claims transformation programs to reduce cycle time, leakage, and fraud while improving customer experience.
* Health and employee-benefits growth strategy for selected European or Asian markets.
* Distribution-channel optimization across agents, brokers, bancassurance partners, and digital direct channels.
* Retail P&C pricing and retention strategy under claims inflation and competitive renewal pressure.
* Operating-model simplification and shared-services redesign across country entities or support functions.
* AI use-case prioritization, governance design, and business-case development for underwriting, claims, and service operations.
* Post-deal separation, transition-management, or integration support tied to portfolio reshaping and partner arrangements.
* Customer cross-sell and lifetime-value analytics across motor, home, health, and protection books.
* Capital-allocation, cost-productivity, and cash-remittance improvement programs for a diversified insurance group.

# AXA group: history and growth

August 16, 2023

[France](/en/taxonomy/term/235)

![Photo credit: Atlas Magazine](/sites/default/files/2011-07/images/focus1_3.png)

The group AXA has been established by way of merging several insurance companies the oldest of which dates back to 1816. Yet, it was not until the 1980s that the brand was affirmed.

![](/sites/default/files/2011-07/images/focus1_3.png)The tremendous rise that will ensue coincides with the arrival of Claude Bébéar, the charismatic head of the company. AXA, headquartered in Paris, which has since become one of the undisputed leaders in the sector with a presence throughout the world. Nevertheless, it was in Normandy that the group kick started.

## The AXA group genesis

Group AXA’s founding company was built in 1816. At that time, Theodore Jacques le Carpentier along with 17 other shareholders, established a mutual insurance company headquartered in Rouen. AXA would inherit both features until 1970. Specializing in non-life insurance, the company was named Compagnie d’Assurances Mutuelles contre l’Incendie (mutual insurance company against fire) in the departments of Seine and Eure. As with any mutual company, policyholders become members, but only for five years. A plate marked with the letters P.A.C.L. (property insured against fire) was then attached to the properties covered by the new insurer.

The first major event the company had to face occurred in 1820. The partial destruction of the Rouen Cathedral by fire was a major loss for the young company.

The industrial revolution of the early nineteenth century has profoundly changed the European economic environment. New companies, such as Providence (1838) and la Paternelle (1843), entered the market and embarked on a competition that the insurer had to cope with as a reality in Rouen. Adolphe Lanne, the group’s manager on duty since 1832, decided to set up two new companies: Mutualité Immobilière(1847) and Mutualité Mobilière specializing in movable estate.

During the following decade, the management extended mutuals’ territoriality throughout France while Mutualité Mobilière set foot on the fire market. In 1881 under the management of Masselin, both companies merged under the name of Ancienne Mutuelle and the new life entity, Mutuelle Vie, came into being. Ancienne Mutuelle’s name would remain unchanged until 1977.

## The AXA group at the period of European wars

![](/sites/default/files/2011-07/images/focus2.jpg)In 1902, all of the offices were gathered in Rouen. Twenty years later, the group embarked on motor insurance through Ancienne Mutuelle Accidents. Its success was immediate and considerably contributed to the profits realized thereafter.

In 1944, Gaston Payenneville, the company’s chairman since 1913, died in his office after a bombing carried out by the Allies. When the war ended, Ancienne Mutuelle was struggling even though Life and Accidents’ entities were less affected.

In 1819 the company, which had 1274 members, paid its first loss amounting to 7.5 Francs.

The arrival in 1946 of André Sahut d’Izarn will mark the beginning of a revival. The group was dotted with a new structure. Its stable and steady progress had lasted until the 1970s. Meanwhile, a succession of mergers with other mutuals would increase the number of policyholders. Ancienne Mutuelle of Calvados (in 1946), Mutuelle d’Orléans (in 1950), Mutualité Générale Vie, the Participation (in 1954) were pooled under its name. In the mid-1950s, the group Ancienne Mutuelle was made up of eight mutual insurance companies and a few commercial insurance companies, all of which subsidiary at 100%.

## The internationalization of the AXA group

Under the leadership of André Sahut d’ Izarn, the group will, as of 1955, extend to Canada where it primarily targeted the Quebec market.

![Photo credit: Atlas Magazine](/sites/default/files/2011-07/images/focus3.jpg "Photo credit: Atlas Magazine")On the recommendation of a friend, son of the group’s chairman, Claude Bébéar joined the company in 1958 as executive assistant. A few years later, he left France for Canada, where he joined the insurer Provinces-Unis, a subsidiary company of Ancienne Mutuellel where he developed life business. His mandate ended in 1968.

André Sahut d’Izarn passed away in June 1972. In April 1974, a strike hit the entire insurance market for two months. Ancienne Mutuelle was, therefore, paralyzed and a new social policy seemed inevitable. The response came with Claude Bébéar, appointed general manager in 1975. From that date onwards, the history of the group and that of its ambitious leader, known as the insurance "Cowboy" became one. The Nouvel Economiste magazine characterized him as the "avantgardist insurer" in 1988.

Claude Bébéar founded the Ancienne Mutuelle de Réassurance (AM Re) in 1977, itself sprung from Ancienne Mutuelle Transport du Bétail, which was founded in 1939. AM Re became AXA Re in 1989 and was then acquired by Paris Re in 2006.

In 1978, the Compagnie Parisienne de Garantie along with Mutuelle de l’Ouest came under the tutelage of Ancienne Mutuelle. The first will be renamed Mutuelle Parisienne de Garantie, while Ancienne Mutuelle group became Mutuelles Unies. The pool reported a turnover of 160 million EUR in 1980 with 1850 employees worldwide. The overall turnover was then achieved in France.

## The AXA group and the global boom of the 1980s

In 1981 the Left came to power with the election of François Mitterrand. Fearing nationalization then in full swing, Bébéar seized the opportunity of controlling the Drouot Group in 1982. This spectacular acquisition dramatically boosted Mutuelle Unies in the forefront of French private insurers with Claude Bébéar becoming chairman of the group.

![Photo credit: Atlas Magazine](/sites/default/files/2011-07/images/focus4.jpg "Photo credit: Atlas Magazine")In July 1985, the group is officially named AXA, more commonly known "group Bébéar." Its president became CEO, quitting the operational department. In April 1986, AXA purchased the company Présence made up of the companies Providence and Secours The latter, then newly merged, operated respectively in life and non life insurance, owning a large network in Europe and France.

In 1988, AXA group merged with the Compagnie du Midi, whose general manager is Bernard Pagézy. Bernard Pagézy was behind the initiative of fostering cooperation as a move to prevent a takeover by the Italian insurer Generali. Cooperation was shortlived as Claude Bébéar decided to take control of the Compagnie du Midi the following year with the help of Generali itself. AXA became the second French insurer behind Union des Assurances de Paris (UAP). The integration of operations of the Compagnie du Midi, the holding company of Assurances Générales de Paris (AGP), enabled Bébéar to take possession of its enormous international network including Equity & Law, the sixth British insurer.

In February 1989, the group had 42 companies and 16 000 employees. In France, AXA structure shielded it from any threat of hostile takeover thanks to the mutual companies in control of the group. In 1989, Claude Bébéar was the first representative in the world of finance to be distinguished Manager of the Year.

## The AXA group: restructuring of the 1990s and external development

![Image provided to Microsoft by iStockphoto. Used with permission from Microsoft](/sites/default/files/2011-07/images/focus5.jpg "Image provided to Microsoft by iStockphoto. Used with permission from Microsoft")The 1990s was marked by a restructuring move affecting operations in France. Claude Bébéar chose a horizontal organization by merging all its group companies into three units, each of which having its own distribution network. The result was a specialization in three areas: AXA Insurance which includes general agents, Uni Europe comprising insurance brokers and Franklin Assurance which covers other retail operations.

In 1990, 27% of the collected premiums were achieved in France. The group was then well established in Europe but had no presence in U.S.A, the largest market in the world. It was in 1991 that the French insurer set foot there by acquiring a majority stake in American The Equitable, just after its demutualization. This occurred after the failure of AXA to buy Farmers in 1990. The Equitable was then a major life insurer that AXA recapitalized and renamed AXA Equitable in 1997.

In 1995, officials in National Mutual Life Insurance Company, the second life insurance company in Australia and Hong Kong, came into contact with Claude Bébéar to help in the process of demutualization. Their goal was to submit a recovery plan identical to that achieved with The Equitable. An agreement was reached. It allowed AXA to recapitalize the company and take its reins. The French group then got introduced in Asia and Oceania, especially as AXA Life became operational in Japan the same year. In 1999, National Mutual changed its name to AXA Asia Pacific.

The year 1996 stands as a major turning point for the group AXA which launched a takeover bid of UAP, the first French insurance company, whose turnover is twice as important. An exchange offer was signed, making AXA the number one insurer in France and worldwide. This position will nevertheless return a year later to Allianz which purchased AGF. AXA, therefore, doubled its size in France and surpassed critical size in Great Britain, Belgium and Germany. The takeover of UAP allowed it to consolidate its presence in other countries. In 1996 the group entered Morocco with the acquisition of Al Amane.

Other acquisitions occurred in subsequent years: In the UK, Guardian Royal Exchange came into the possession of the French group. Taking advantage of Japan's economic difficulties, AXA set foot in the country’s 13th life company, Nippon Dantai. Other Asian companies were then bought out in China (AXA Minmetals), in Turkey (AXA Oyak), in Lebanon (AXA Middle East).

## The AXA group in the 2000s, post-Claude Bébéar era

As he had announced, Claude Bébéar yielded his position as president of the management board to Henri de Castries in 2000. He then became chairman of the supervisory board. The beginnings of the new man at the head of the company were marked by the New York attacks whose losses reached 650 million EUR (612 million USD). The consolidation of the group's positions in this market was, nonetheless, pursued with further acquisitions including that of the Mutual of New York in 2004. In 2002, 87% of turnover was generated abroad.

Meanwhile, development in emerging countries became a priority, particularly in Asia:

* opening of an entity in Canton (2004)
* establishment of a joint venture with bank Mandiri in Indonesia (2004) and acquisition of MLC Indonesia (2005). Following these transactions, AXA became the third insurer in the country
* association with local banks in the Philippines and Thailand (2004)
* establishment of AXA Tech in India (2005)
* establishment in Saudi Arabia with AXA Gulf (2005)

The group's strategy was somewhat different in South America:

* withdrawal from the Chilean market in 2002
* withdrawal from Uruguay in 2005
* presence limited to assistance insurance only in Argentina and Brazil
* acquisition of the largest insurer in the Mexican market ING Seguros in 2008

In Europe, AXA took control of the Portuguese company Seguro Directo (2005) and withdrew from the Netherlands in 2007. Switzerland remained a prime target with the acquisition of Winterthur in 2006 and Nationale Suisse Assurance in 2007.

The group announced in early June 2011 its withdrawal from the Canadian market with the sale of its subsidiary company AXA Canada to Intact Financial for 2.7 billion USD.
